View image in fullscreen
The report was launched at the UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey on Monday.  Photograph: Mehmet Ali Ozcan/Anadolu/Getty Images


AI models ‘weak and fallible’ on climate science, UN-backed study reports


While mostly accurate describing simple facts, models pivoted to denial and wrong answers when challenged 
 
 
Cop31 live – latest updates  




Artificial intelligence models can quickly turn into climate crisis deniers at the mildest challenge from users, according to a new UN-backed study.
While AI models can accurately confirm simple facts about climate change, eight times out of 10 when they pivoted to a wrong answer, they did so “at the very first sign that the user mildly disagreed” to confirm incorrect statements such as “CO2 is not the main driver of climate change”.

The report uncovered a strong tendency for AI models to be sycophantic, meaning the model is more interested in pleasing the user than standing by facts – an issue identified when people turn to AI chatbots for personal advice.
The report from Unesco and University College London was launched at the UN climate summit in Turkey on Monday, revealing the results of tests on 15 of the world’s most popular AI models.
Leona Verdadero, Unesco’s lead author of the report, said: “AI is not neutral. When it comes to how it responds to the user, it will be pushed to align with the users’ preference instead of sticking up for the facts. The fact they could so easily abandon truth and be more agreeable to a user’s [misinformation] shows it is weak and fallible.”
When AI was asked how a single climate policy would work, such as a carbon tax, the models were mostly accurate. But when asked how two climate policies could work together, accuracy collapsed to no better than random guessing, the researchers said.
Dr María Pérez-Ortiz, of UCL’s department of computer science and a senior author of the report, said: “AI systems are remarkably good at explaining scientific knowledge, but this can give us a false sense of their capabilities. Our findings show why we must be careful when moving from asking AI what we know about climate change to asking what we should do about it.”


View image in fullscreen
The report was published the same day Turkey, the Cop31 hosts, launched the AI Antalya pledge to make AI ‘part of the climate solution’. Photograph: Mehmet Ali Ozcan/Anadolu/Getty Images
AI models also had a language problem. Accuracy was scored at 88% for people using English, and comparatively high in Spanish, French and Portuguese.
Responses were less accurate for people speaking Hindi, Bengali and Urdu, and the worst for Swahili speakers, at 78%. This was particularly important, the report authors said, because those languages were spoken in places among the hardest hit by the climate crisis.

Surge of US datacenters adds equivalent of Denmark’s annual emissions, study finds


‘Hyperscaler’ datacenters across country draw upon dirtier power sources to meet vast energy needs, research shows




The frantic buildout of “hyperscaler” datacenters in the US has collectively caused planet-heating emissions of about the same scale as Denmark emits in a year, new research has found.
In that period 403 “hyperscalers” – the largest datacenters used primarily to handle the growth of artificial intelligence – emitted about 25.7m metric tons of carbon dioxide, according to the study.

This is equivalent to the entire annual carbon pollution of Denmark, a country of 6 million people, and is about two to three times more than a previous estimate of hyperscale emissions in 2018. The latest research, published in Nature Sustainability, found that these datacenters were responsible for about 1.8% of total US electricity consumption.
Researchers said this vast datacenter energy demand, centered on states such as Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa, is almost certainly a conservative estimate. The study used federal government data to determine emissions from the facilities over a year until April 2025. Since then, the rapid expansion of datacenters has only accelerated further.







Several Democrats renew calls for datacenter pauses after blue wave

Read more
“There has been an explosion in these datacenters and the CO2 emissions are pretty substantial,” said Francesca Dominici, a professor of biostatistics at Harvard University and co-author of the study, which was led by Gianluca Guidi. “Since 2025 there have been many, many more datacenters so we need to think of this level of emissions as a lower bound. This is something that needs study and for policymakers to think about how to do this in a responsible way.”
Datacenters use an enormous amount of energy – the new study estimates the hyperscale group consumed 68 to 99 terawatt-hours of electricity over the year – and largely draws upon dirtier sources of power to meet this demand.


More than half of the generation used by hyperscalers came from the fossil fuels that are dangerously overheating our planet, the research found. The growth of AI is being underpinned by a rise in new gas-fired power, sometimes built at the site of the facilities themselves, which is being favored over installed renewables such as solar and wind.
“Sadly, it doesn’t surprise me that the majority of hyperscale datacenters rely on fossil fuels for their power generation despite the profound and lasting climate and health impacts that could be, and should be, avoided,” said Gina McCarthy, a former climate adviser to Joe Biden’s admin

Passing bill to speed up gas projects and datacenters would be ‘serious mistake’, Al Gore says


Former vice-president at Cop31 urges lawmakers to rethink contentious bipartisan Baaja bill advanced by the US Senate




It would be a “serious mistake” to pass a contentious bipartisan bill to speed up energy projects and datacenters that has divided Democrats and environmentalists, Al Gore said.
The legislation, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (Baaja), will make it easier to build large infrastructure projects in the US, from oil and gas pipelines and datacenters to crucial clean energy components such as solar and wind power and transmission lines, scaling back environmental protections and legal challenges in order to do so.

The permitting bill, devised by a group of Republicans and Democrats, passed a procedural vote in the US Senate last week, but has split Democrats and green groups over whether its trade-offs are worth supporting. Gore, the former US vice-president, said he is opposed to the bill and urged a rethink.



“I think it would be a serious mistake, particularly in the wake of the astonishing election results last week,” Gore, referencing Democrats’ sweeping midterm wins, said at the Cop31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.
“The fact that President Trump endorsed it enthusiastically is a clue, the fact that the American Petroleum Institute is giving out free tacos in Washington to support it is also a clue. I hope they reconsider because I think it would be a very, very serious mistake.”

articles.jina_text:
Imran Lodhi is a university lecturer with a doctorate in climate change and sustainable development. The 41-year-old was living in Dera Ghazi Khan, a city in south-western Punjab, when floods devastated provinces across Pakistan. Climate change made the monsoon rainfall that caused the floods more intense.
In 2022, I was living in an area that had less risk of flooding. I had a small child and my PhD thesis was just a few weeks away. I tried to avoid flood news on social media until I saw a picture of a two-year-old girl who was buried in mud. It was probably her last breath. She died after that. That was the turning point.


View image in fullscreen
Imran Lodhi immediately rallied friends to help victims of the devastating flooding across Pakistan in 2022. Photograph: Zoral Naik
I immediately called my friends, six to seven people, in a mosque. I talked to them: “We don’t know what to do, but at least we can start from somewhere.” Initially, it was food. We hired some commercial cooks.
We planned to work only in villages close to our city. A lot of people were taking refuge in nearby high places, high enough that the water did not reach them. On the first day we went with some food to the nearest village.
When the rain is over, the sun comes out. Usually, it’s a good sign. But, in those areas, it didn’t feel good. It felt like it opened a scar. The pain that was hiding somehow had become open. It was like being naked. I could see trolleys, tractors, vehicles and homes all drowned in the flood. There was nothing from the government, nothing from any development sector. There was no camp. People were just living under open skies.
Men felt that their women being in an open place was a kind of emotional damage for them. It was not normal for most of the people here. Many women never came out. They came out for their work, the agriculture work, but not sitting that openly among the public. Their hair was full of dust and dry mud. Their clothes had a heavy layer of dry mud; no shoes on their feet. Mothers were not breastfeeding. Babies crying for milk, and the milk was not there. Mothers trying to soothe them with fake sounds.
The cows did not have feed and were not giving milk. Many of the animals were lost, their bodies wide open, decomposed. Then the water, which stayed there for a week, started to smell very bad. There was no good smell.


View image in fullscreen
Families displaced by flooding in Balochistan province were forced to live in tents on causeways and other higher ground. Photograph: Fida Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
We prepared food in the morning. Then we prepared food at lunchtime. We generally finished distributing food around 8pm. One night it was 11pm and we thought some people might not have food. So we just cooked some food late at night and went to every camp.

Great Britain’s oldest renewables projects could rake in nearly £9bn next year


Subsidy scheme, which is paid via taxes and energy bills, must be reformed, ECU analysis finds 
 
 
Business live – latest updates  




Great Britain’s oldest renewable energy projects are likely to rake in a near £9bn windfall next year because of soaring market prices, according to independent analysis.
The research has revealed that almost a third of the UK’s wind and solar farms that rely on the government’s legacy renewables subsidy scheme are in line for soaring subsidy payments as officials grapple with plans to lower the country’s energy costs.








Greenpeace boulders may delay building of £12bn windfarms in North Sea

Read more
Renewable energy projects built between 2003 and 2014 are expected to claim £4.5bn in subsidies over the next financial year, on top of £4.2bn in wholesale market revenue. The analysis showed developers will receive almost 50% more than before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent gas prices soaring in 2022.
The analysis by the Energy Competitiveness Unit (ECU), a non-partisan research and policy project, said the legacy support scheme – which is paid via taxes and energy bills – must be reformed “if we are serious about getting costs of the electricity system down in the short and medium term”.
Unlike newer renewable energy projects that earn fixed-price subsidies for their generation, older projects access support via the renewables obligation (RO) scheme, which provides payments on top of what developers earn via the wholesale market, meaning that higher gas market prices lead to higher subsidy costs for renewables.
The scheme was credited with kickstarting the UK’s renewable energy industry when it was put in place almost 25 years ago, but the ECU said it “has been allowed to persist unsustainably”.
Andrew O’Brien, the ECU director, told the Guardian that the rise in wholesale prices over recent years has meant that many renewable energy developers are earning “well above what they could reasonably have expected” when first taking the decision to invest in the projects.


View image in fullscreen
A solar farm near Andover in Hampshire. Photograph: Toby Melville/Reuters
The government announced last year that it would remove three-quarters of the RO scheme’s costs from home energy bills, and move these levies into general taxation from April 2026 to help temper the steep rise in energy bills.

articles.jina_text:
The Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34.
While the diplomatic picture is less bleak than it might have been, the threat level remains high and rising. António Guterres used his last Cop as UN secretary general to issue a pithy warning that “it’s make or bake time”. With the latest analysis pointing to heating of 2.7C by the end of the century – far beyond the 1.5C target in the Paris agreement – governments face another crunch moment: by pivoting away from fossil fuels, they can still avert the most dangerous impacts. Yet the UK’s Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to make the trip to Turkey; the French and German leaders chose to attend an EU summit in Dublin instead.



View image in fullscreen
António Guterres. Photograph: AFP/Getty
Warnings of mounting risks, unprecedented heat and disasters such as August’s glacier collapse on the Nepal-Tibet border can engender a sense of paralysis or unreality. The leaders of both host countries prompted anger last week: the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, publicly extolled his country’s oil reserves, while Australia’s Anthony Albanese failed to mention fossil fuels in his speech. But for all its flaws, the UN climate process remains crucial. There is no other mechanism to broker a global green transition.
Mr Burnham’s appointment of a climate security adviser, Madeleine Alessandri, should focus minds in the UK. Kemi Badenoch’s rejection of net zero has undermined an important cross‑party consensus. Ministers, who must soon make a decision on Rosebank oil and gas field, must realise that economic damage caused by the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced would dwarf any benefits. Governments of countries that are far poorer than the UK cannot be expected to turn away from coal and oil if rich countries keep investing.


A resolution to derive 35% of energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 will be agreed this week if objections from fossil fuel producers can be overcome. Attempts to undermine the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change must also be resisted. It provides the science on which the process depends. Increased accountability on climate finance is urgently needed too. Poor countries cannot be expected to put up with endless delays.

The people of Papua New Guinea’s Ahus Island spent decades preparing for the growing effects of the climate crisis, building sea walls and installing water tanks. Photograph: Bing Lin
View image in fullscreen
The people of Papua New Guinea’s Ahus Island spent decades preparing for the growing effects of the climate crisis, building sea walls and installing water tanks. Photograph: Bing Lin


The creeks are dry, the rain is contaminated and food is scarce. What lies ahead for the people of Ahus Island?


A small island community spent years preparing for the climate crisis. Now they have no water – and nowhere else to go




Visitors are few to the island of Ahus, a tiny atoll in the north of Papua New Guinea’s sprawling archipelago.
But Prof Josh Cinner and his team are well known. The ocean sustainability researchers have been visiting the island for a quarter of a century, their arrivals usually heralded with a modest ceremony, dancing and shared food and drink.

The last time they arrived – in October – it was “a ghost town”.
“The research team wondered if everyone was off-island,” Cinner, director of the University of Sydney’s Thriving Oceans Research Hub, tells the Guardian, “but then they would look in the houses and just see people lying on the ground of their huts, trying to conserve energy, trying to conserve water.


View image in fullscreen
Michelle Suri says there is not enough clean water and almost every household is going hungry. Photograph: Bing Lin
“School was cut to a half day … because it was too hot for the kids to be in school, and there’s been a massive reduction in fishing. Fishing is very physical, and people just don’t have enough water, they don’t have enough energy, and it’s just too hot to go fishing.”


PNG, and a huge swathe of south-east Asia, is in the grip of a brutal “supercharged” El Niño event, that has brought soaring temperatures, vanishingly little rain and widespread food and water shortages.
The drought has meant that on the neighbouring, larger island of Manus, there is little food on sale at the markets. But the fishers of Ahus have few fish to trade anyway.
The intensely interconnected economy which has sustained these islands for generations is breaking down.
“When it finally did rain, everyone was excited,” Cinner says. “But there’s all this smoke from the bushfires in Borneo, it’s just haze. So when the rain came, it was acid rain.”

Instead of harvesting the water, villagers in Ahus were forced to hurriedly disconnect their catchment systems, so as not to poison what little drinking water they did have.
“What could prepare you for this? Even the rain in a drought is toxic,” Cinner says. “What do you do? The wells are dry. They have to paddle across the channel to try to get water on the mainland [Manus Island], but they don’t have rights to the water there. And the creeks there are drying out.”

articles.jina_text:
The UN’s annual climate conference began in Turkey this week. Reporting from the event can be gruelling work – but it’s also crucial. 




They are counting on you not to read our coverage of the Cop31 climate talks. Fossil fuel companies, climate science deniers, petrostates, far right populists … They want you to think the negotiations are too intractable, the progress too halting, the issues too complex, too tortuous, too pointless, TL;DR.
But as the UN’s 31st annual climate conference got underway in Antalya, Turkey this week, our journalists have been going to great lengths to help you understand why the talks remain urgent, crucial and – hopefully – consequential. As well as helping you follow the agreements reached and progress made during the two week summit, they have also been highlighting what’s at stake.








What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?

Read more
Covering a Cop is gruelling work. The negotiations are by definition difficult: representatives from almost every country in the world attempt to thrash out consensus agreements and roadmaps for confronting humanity’s greatest threat. There are also practical hurdles, with 70,000 registered delegates at this year’s summit, packed venues and tangled schedules. On Tuesday morning, the Guardian’s live blog from the conference also chronicled the odyssey of our journalist Graham Readfearn as he struggled for three and a half hours just to get to the venue on one of the special Cop31 buses that got caught in the Antalya traffic.
Graham’s quest wasn’t a metaphor – it was just one of many practical challenges reporters face when covering a Cop (which stands for Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change). These challenges are that much harder for smaller media organisations from poorer nations that are particularly vulnerable to the impacts of the climate emergency.
I asked some of our journalists ​why it’s such an important conference to cover and the challenges they face reporting from it.


Ajit Niranjan 
European environment correspondent
“The hardest thing about covering Cop is satisfying the many different audiences who turn to our coverage during this chaotic fortnight. For the tens of thousands of people attending the summit, we offer a close-up view of the diplomatic spats (and rare breakthroughs) that have sweeping consequences for humanity and the other species with which we share this planet. And for the average Guardian reader, who cares about the climate but may not need the minutiae of UN diplomacy, we mix key takeaways from the negotiations with the most riveting, heartbreaking, terrifying and encouraging stories about the climate crisis. It’s a rare moment during the year when climate change is in the spotlight, and we want to serve as many readers as we can.”

articles.jina_text:
The latest Met Office forecast suggests hill snow across North Wales, northern England and Scotland from Tuesday, along with plunging temperatures throughout the UK. 
As winter approaches, many households will be thinking about turning their heating up to keep the cold at bay.  
But as energy costs continue to put pressure on household budgets — with the typical household paying around £144 a month for gas and electricity — finding ways to stay warm without sending bills soaring is more important than ever. 

 

Thankfully however, there are a few simple things you can do before the cold snap hits to improve your heating efficiency without spending a penny. 

 
Reduce your boiler flow temperature  
This tiny tweak can save £100 a year if you have a combi boiler – and you won’t notice the difference. 
Your boiler comes with a default ‘flow temperature’, which controls how hot the water is when it leaves your boiler to heat your radiators. 
According to Zoe Morris, savings expert at VoucherCodes.co.uk, most boilers are set to run at 70°C to 80°C, but they actually work more efficiently (and cheaply) at a lower temperature. 
‘By reducing the flow temperature to around 60°C, your boiler doesn’t have to work as hard, which means it uses less gas and, therefore, costs less to run,’ she told Metro. 
Lowering this setting means your boiler runs in its most efficient mode – known as condensing mode – which can significantly cut energy use. 
If you’re not sure how to do it, check the Money Saving Boiler Challenge from innovation charity Nesta or search online for videos that show your particular brand of boiler. 
 
   
Just a tiny tweak can save more than you would think (Picture: Getty Images) 
Get your radiators ready 
Cleaning and bleeding your radiators will help them work more efficiently, meaning you won’t have to use as much energy to get your rooms warm. 
British Gas repair engineer Sunny Solanky explains that pockets of air can build up inside radiators, preventing them from heating your home evenly. 
‘If you notice the top of your radiators feel cooler than the bottom, switch the system off and let it cool,’ he says. 
You can then use a radiator key to carefully release the trapped air, allowing hot water to circulate properly again. 

 
It’s also worth looking at what’s surrounding your radiators, as furniture can prevent heat from circulating around the room. 
Sebrina McCullough, of the Money Wellness blog, recommends leaving a little breathing room between your radiators and any furniture. 
She told Metro: ‘You should leave around 6in to 12in between any furniture and radiators to ensure free movement of air and circulation of heat.’ 
Lower the radiator valves in less-used rooms 
If you have thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) fitted to your radiators, adjusting them could save you up to £40 a year, according to Smart Energy GB. 
These valves allow you to control the temperature of individual rooms, meaning you don’t have to heat every corner

articles.jina_text:
A council leader has told of his relief that he no longer resides on a council estate now deemed a major flood risk zone. 




Barking and Dagenham Labour council leader Dominic Twomey has said he is “glad” he no longer lives on the Rylands Estate in Oval Road North, where he called home for “many years”.








He added he “would never have imagined” it would be part of an area at risk of flooding.




Cllr Twomey said: “I’m glad I no longer live where I used to live.




“Some of the areas here – middle of the borough – are not at risk from the rivers.




“But that flooding because of other drainage issues is quite a worrying development, particularly with the changing weather that’s now coming forward, you can see that flooding through drainage issues more and more and more.”




The estate is one of four areas in Barking and Dagenham borough facing a “significant” flood risk, according to a new council flood strategy.




The flooding risk at Rylands Estate comes from water diverted by flood defences at the River Beam and Wantz Stream, according to a new draft flood risk management strategy.




The strategy says that “properties at risk lie mainly on Ballards Close, Ballards Road and the eastern end of School Road” while “several further properties on Oval Road North” are also at risk.


Oval Road North, Dagenham 
Google




It adds that 16 homes could be flooded in a one-in-30 year flooding event.




Homes are at less risk from flooding around Parsloes Park – 76 homes could be flooded in a one-in-75 year event.












Elsewhere in the borough, some 48 homes are at risk around Heathway Industrial Estate – mainly on Rainham Road North and Panyers Gardens – because they sit on the historic path of the Wantz Stream, which is now diverted underground in a culvert.




Westrow Drive is also at risk of flooding by water diverted by flood defences elsewhere, with 18 homes at risk. 








The draft strategy says surface water flowing towards the Mayes Brook is blocked by a flood defence, causing it to “pond in the residential area behind it”.




The draft flood risk management strategy proposes four projects to protect homes in those areas. These include building a flood bank in Old Dagenham Park to protect Rylands Estate, at a cost of around £212,337.

The council has applied for grant funding for a flood water storage scheme in Rainham Road North.

Strongest El Niño in centuries adds urgency to UN climate talks as vulnerable countries face ‘compounding’ crises




If the galloping pace of the climate crisis isn’t enough to spur countries to act at UN climate talks under way in Turkey, there is another major threat heightening its havoc: the strongest El Niño event in at least 1,000 years.
The “jaw-dropping” El Niño, a naturally recurring phenomenon where the eastern Pacific heats up every few years with temporary but global implications, has provided added urgency to wrangling at the Cop31 summit over climate funding for vulnerable countries that are having to scramble to respond.

Already, warping global weather patterns have fuelled huge wildfires and crop failures in Indonesia, coastal inundation in the US, severe drought in Sudan and severe flooding in countries including Ecuador and Somalia. “We are supercharging our weather and El Niño will be a risk multiplier,” said Celeste Saulo, secretary-general of the World Meteorological Organization.

Last year, wealthy countries agreed to triple the amount of adaptation finance to poorer countries most vulnerable to floods heatwaves, wildfires and other damaging climate impacts. Yet just a fraction of the $305bn a year needed by 2035 is being delivered, with rich nations consistently lagging in providing climate finance.
This shortfall will be sharply felt in the coming year as El Niño takes its toll. “It’s so frustrating as countries that have done the least to cause climate change are being left with bills we can’t afford,” said Jetn̄il-Kijiner.

Pat McFadden, the Work and Pensions Secretary, has said “we have to reorientate the system” to help young people out of unemployment.



Ahead of the Milburn review set to be published this week, McFadden told Sky News there must be a “fundamental reset” to implement the report’s findings.



This includes cutting welfare benefits to redirect the funds towards supporting young pople into work or training.



“If you have extra costs because of a condition, there will also be an extra cost benefit, and people will get investment in support upfront, as well as the benefit figures,” McFadden said.



“You’ve also got to consider the long-term consequences of being on those benefits. One of the most remarkable statistics I’ve come across in the last year is that if a young person goes on to long-term sickness benefits at the age of 20, they’re more likely to celebrate their 30th birthday than to have had a steady job in between.”

Legal age of consent being 16 is ‘bane of our lives’ says social worker and campagner 

Layla Stone, who founded the group and has spent her career as a child protection social worker, told the Press Association: “Adult relationships with 16 and 17-year-olds have always been a feature of my work, and something that for most child protection professionals, is the bane of our lives.
“Which is that you can disrupt and protect a 15-year-old from relationships with much older adults, but as soon as they turn 16, your powers of protection are almost completely gone.
“It is very difficult to disrupt a relationship between somebody who is classed as legally able to consent in the law, but yet still classed as a child.”
Ms Stone also referred to the fact that it is illegal in the UK to be in possession of an indecent image of anyone under the age of 18.
She said: “The real kicker for us is the fact that at 16, 17, if an adult was in possession of indecent images of you, that adult would be in possession of child sexual abuse material and could be punished under the law.
“But the same adult could have sex with the same child and it would be perfectly legal.
“So you recognise them as children in sexual abuse material terms, but not as children when adults are actually having physical sex with them.”

LGBTQ+ protesters defy crackdown in Turkey to march with Cop31 activists


Civil society campaigners form protective cordon around LGBTQ+ campaigners as they unfurl flags and placards




Queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march on Saturday in the city hosting this year’s UN climate summit.
Turkey’s LGBTQ+ groups have faced increased persecution since September, with police targeting activists in their homes or at the offices of the NGOs that advocate for their rights.

But on Saturday afternoon, civil society campaigners from around the world that had gathered in Antalya for tCop31 formed a cordon around them as they unfurled rainbow flags.
Őzgǔr, a 20-year-old Turkish LGBTQ+ activist, marched defiantly with a rainbow flag wrapped over her shoulders. She said holding the flag “feels a bit dangerous” and that usually police would not allow it.
“It feels like I am living in a prison in this country. I am running all the time,” she said. “We can do this because the eyes of the international media are here.”


View image in fullscreen
Environmentalists hold a rally in Antalya as the city hosts the Cop31 summit this week. Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters
Another activist, who gave her name only as Beren, added: “I feel very excited about being able to wave the flag, but I would love my friend to be here. She is detained right now because she is trans.”


Turkish police ran a massive security operation around the march. Attenders were frisked twice and had bags searched on the way into Aydin Kanza Park, where the protest gathered. The entire route was cordoned off with steel barriers to prevent anyone entering or leaving until the end.
Police examined the slogans on protesters’ placards and in some cases photographed them. “We have all been told we have to bring our passports,” said Asad Rehman, the chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. “Our bags are being searched.
“It’s a very, very difficult time for Turkish movements who have faced a wave of repression. And so this is an important moment for us as the international movement to create some space for Turkish voices to be heard.”
The inclusion of LGBTQ+ activists on the march was carefully planned in advance. Protest organisers ensured that flags would be available, but they were not unfurled until the activists were safely surrounded by civil society groups and media.

As Cop31 continues and scientists warn that climate breakdown may be accelerating, the Guardian looks back at a year of droughts, fires and floods as a reminder that, unless the world takes urgent action to cut emissions, this disastrous year will be one of the best of the rest of our lives.

On Sunday, the cold weather will give way to milder conditions, with temperatures expected to stay above freezing in the morning. 
Sunshine is forecast in the east in the morning and across the far north and west later in the day. 
Conditions are otherwise expected to be cloudy and breezy with outbreaks of rain, some heavy, and potential hill snow in the north. 
According to the Met Office, the current cold weather has been caused by developments in the troposphere, the lowest part of the atmosphere. High pressure has changed the UK’s wind direction, bringing in colder air from the Arctic.  
Milder and wetter weather is expected over the coming weeks as Atlantic low-pressure systems bring in rain and stronger winds.  
It follows an exceptionally dry start to November, particularly across drought-affected areas of England. 
What is the outlook for the rest of winter? 
While it is impossible to reliably forecast the weather for the coming winter, climate scientists say there is potential for extreme cold in the UK due to an event happening right now in the Arctic.



 
Each year powerful winds, known as the polar vortex, develop high in the stratosphere over the Arctic during the colder months.  
When these winds weaken, they can bring unusually cold temperatures to the UK, as happened during the Beast from the East in 2018. 
The polar vortex is currently experiencing an exceptionally early and unusual disruption, which could bring colder weather to the UK in December. The Met Office is monitoring the situation, but said any impact would be likely to be short-lived. 
However, current long range forecasts predict the polar vortex will weaken again in January or February, which could bring more extreme cold around that time.  
Many climate scientists believe this could be a result of the Super El Niño currently developing in the Pacific Ocean, which is expected to wreak havoc in many parts of the globe.   
El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon involving the significant warming of ocean water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. It occurs every two to seven years and influences weather patterns across the world.

articles.jina_text:
Boulders weighing up to 2 tonnes being dropped onto the seabed in the North Sea by Greenpeace Photograph: Andrew McConnell/PA
View image in fullscreen
Boulders weighing up to 2 tonnes being dropped onto the seabed in the North Sea by Greenpeace Photograph: Andrew McConnell/PA


Greenpeace boulders may delay building of £12bn windfarms in North Sea


Activists dumped rocks off Norfolk coast on site of Burnham-backed project in protest against seabed trawling




The giant offshore windfarms backed by Andy Burnham this week may face unexpected stumbling blocks after Greenpeace activists unwittingly dumped about 15 tonnes of boulders on to the site as part of a campaign against seabed trawling in the North Sea.
Greenpeace created the “boulder barrier” to safeguard harbour porpoises off the Norfolk coast by dropping giant stone blocks, each weighing up to 2 tonnes, on to the sea floor to prevent a method of fishing known as bottom trawling.

The barrier will pose an additional challenge for the green energy developers because most of the boulders were dropped on to the site earmarked for one of the UK’s biggest planned windfarms, known as the Norfolk Vanguard project.





Greenpeace campaigners drop boulders onto the seabed to create anti-trawler barrier
Greenpeace began dumping boulders on to the site, without consent from the marine authority, days before the prime minister told the Cop31 summit that the UK would invest £1bn of public money in the Vanguard West and Vanguard East windfarms in what is believed to be the biggest investment of its kind in UK history.
The Guardian understands that Greenpeace checked the seabed for any existing cables, pipelines or shipwrecks, but it was not aware of the plans to build the Vanguard East windfarm.

The creation of the underwater barrier in one of “the most heavily trawled” areas of the southern North Sea was timed to coincide with the premiere of the BBC’s Blue Planet III documentary, narrated by Sir David Attenborough.


Some boulders bear the signatures of celebrities including Simon Pegg and Benedict Cumberbatch, who have voiced marine conservation documentaries, and agreed to support the Greenpeace campaign.
However, they are likely to be removed within months after renewable energy developers agreed a £12bn deal alongside the UK government to begin building the offshore windfarm next year. Industrial fishing activities, including bottom trawling, are also likely to move elsewhere to avoid the construction area.
The Guardian understands that the offshore wind developer, the German utility company RWE, is in talks with Greenpeace to verify the exact placement of the boulders so that they can update the seabed surveys they began last summer. The company is also investigating any potential impact to the construction of the project or its undersea cables.

Global heating and the El Nino weather pattern made the hot, dry conditions behind this year's wildfires in Indonesia far more severe, an analysis has found.
Researchers from Indonesia, the US, the Netherlands, Sweden and the UK analysed rainfall, temperatures and short spells of hot, dry air in three regions covering parts of Sumatra, Borneo and Java between July and October.
They found that El Nino, the natural warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean that disrupts weather worldwide, was the main cause of the severe lack of rain, cutting rainfall between July and October by about 50 per cent. 




Human-caused global heating, driven mainly by the burning of fossil fuels, was the primary driver of high temperatures between August and October, making the season's heat about 1.6C hotter. El Nino added about 0.3C and made the heat about 11 times more likely.
The study by World Weather Attribution (WWA), an international collaboration of scientists that assesses how the climate crisis influences extreme weather, was published on Thursday. 

The study says observations suggest the climate crisis also reduced rainfall by about 15 per cent, but climate models did not reproduce that effect, and the authors describe the role of the climate crisis in the lack of rain as uncertain.


The researchers also assessed vapour pressure deficit (VPD), a measure of how strongly the air draws moisture from plants and soil, in kilopascals (kPa), a unit of pressure. They examined the highest seven-day average of daily maximum values in the season, which indicates sustained spells of hot, dry air that often lead to fires. 
Human-caused warming made such conditions about three times more likely and raised their intensity by about 0.4 kPa, while El Nino made them about five times more likely and raised their intensity by about 0.6 kPa. The authors describe the figures as conservative because the models used include some that do not represent El Nino well, and say the conditions seen this year are relatively common in years with a similar El Nino.


"Our analysis shows that climate change acts as a force multiplier during El Nino years. When a strong El Nino hits, global warming makes the resulting fire weather significantly hotter, drier, and harder to contain," said Dr Theodore Keeping, an extreme weather and wildfire researcher at Imperial College London and an author of the study.

For the world’s least developed countries – many of which are also suffering from debt crises, and unable to apply for loans – the core message at Cop31 is simple: much more money, supplied in the form of grants, is needed to address extreme weather resulting from climate change. 
“This is not a negotiable position for us: we did not create the climate crisis, we did not choose to have these challenges face us, and now we cannot afford to address its impacts,” says Chiku Kilembe, who is attending Cop31 as part of Malawi’s climate finance negotiating team. “For countries like ours, which has quite a severe debt situation, we really need more grants.” 
The problem is, in the wake of cuts to foreign aid from wealthy nations like the US and UK, there is much less cash available at the Cop. Last year, foreign aid fell by 23 per cent to its lowest level in a decade – spearheaded by a 56.9 per cent cut from the US – even as climate impacts have continued to escalate. 




“Climate finance is about three things: quantity, quality, and access. So if you reduce the aid budget, you are reducing the quantity,” says Debbie Hillier, policy lead on UN climate negotiations at the development charity Prosper Global. “Clearly aid reductions are bad news here.” 
The chasm between money available and money required has created something of an impasse in negotiations at Cop31. This is further complicated by the fact that the list of “Annex II” countries who are officially required to provide money in the UN system is fixed on terms devised in 1992. This means that newly-wealthy countries – including China, the UAE, South Korea and Singapore – do not officially have to provide climate finance, while the likes of Greece and Portugal are required to.

“European countries might have a lot of publicity about their cuts, but a lot of them are still doing a very good job, while a lot of very rich countries are not doing anything like what they should,” suggests Sarah Colenbrander, director of climate and environment at think tank ODI Global.

articles.title: What could El Niño mean for winter weather in the US and Canada?
articles.raw_rss: El Niño winters typically bring more rain in the southern USA and drier, warmer conditions further north but the impacts on snowfall are complex.

articles.jina_text:
The developing El Niño - already the strongest on record by some measures - continues to grow and could have profound effects on the weather across North America this autumn and winter.
The naturally-occurring climate phenomenon sees trade winds over the Pacific Ocean, which usually blow from east to west, weakening or reversing with warm water instead spreading eastwards.
This releases heat into the atmosphere which can drive major shifts in global weather patterns.
Impacts in the US and Canada are varied, with a greater chance of a warm and dry winter in northern areas and more risk of flooding rain further south.
There is also some evidence that El Niño can increase the likelihood of disruption to the stratospheric polar vortex which can, in turn, bring snowfall later in winter.
No two El Niños are the same and the impacts are not guaranteed - the odds are just shifted in favour of certain outcomes.






UN warns of 'supersized' El Niño as countries prepare for impact





3 September



Wet in the south




The eastward shift of warm ocean waters associated with El Niño can cause the Pacific jet stream to move south and extend eastwards, directing rain-bearing weather systems across the southern USA.
This typically leads to wetter winters during El Niño years.




Image source, BBC / NOAA
Image caption, 

The likely impacts of El Niño on winter weather vary across different parts of North America.




The latest three month forecast, external from the US National Weather Service (NWS) suggests this is a likely outcome for the winter of 2026-2027.
South-eastern states, including Florida, Georgia and the Carolinas, have the greatest chance of seeing above-average rainfall.
The El Niño winter of 1997-1998 brought significant flooding in the south-east and spun up tornadoes for Florida.



Risk of west coast floods




Image source, Caroline Brehman/EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock
Image caption, 

Severe flooding hit Long Beach, California in February 2024.




California could well find itself in the firing line with forecasts suggesting a wet winter is likely. 
Governor Gavin Newsom has already declared a state of emergency, external ahead of anticipated floods and mudslides.
Areas scarred by recent wildfires are particularly susceptible, with the effects of climate change exacerbating the risks.
Many past El Niños have been wet here, with winter 2023-2024 bringing relief from drought. However this is not always the case. In the strong El Niño of 2015-2016, California actually had below-average rainfall.
Coastal erosion and large waves could be worsened by a rise in the overall sea level driven by so-called Kelvin waves.
This is where ocean water which sloshes eastwards across the Pacific due to El Niño reaches the west coast of the Americas, where it can travel no further.
It causes a large-scale wave which then spreads along the coast over a period of weeks and months, raising sea levels by 15cm (6in) or more.

Guterres warned that climate change drives geopolitical instability and poverty while urging wealthy nations to provide promised finance to vulnerable countries.
 The world must immediately and drastically cut fossil fuel emissions to avert the most catastrophic effects of climate change, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said Friday at his final climate summit, urging the world to “follow the science” and face hard facts.
“You cannot build peace on a burning planet," Guterres told reporters, stressing that climate change is central to the U.N.'s work because it contributes to geopolitical instability by driving hunger and displacement, pushing countries into debt and fueling competition for land and water.
“You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it,” he added. “You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends. And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did least to cause this crisis suffer first and worst.”





World leaders meeting in Turkey for the annual U.N. climate talks are trying to reach consensus on concrete actions to address climate change — which is fueling more intense and deadly heat waves, droughts, floods and other disasters — and help countries at greatest risk, including island nations that also are losing land to rising seas.

Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both 

Jonathan Freedland



The environmental and economic dilemmas he faces are formidable but, with a bold plan, he could set an example for leaders around the world




For politicians of the centre-left especially, it’s the great dilemma of the age. How do you do what everyone can see is essential to save the planet from boiling – even as your voters demand action to get the economy growing and to make life more affordable? Plenty of activists will tell you there’s no contradiction, that tackling the climate crisis makes economic as well as ecological sense and, in the long term, you know they’re right. But you don’t live in the long term. You’re running the government right now and facing several unavoidable, binary choices.
Andy Burnham is a prime example. This week, he addressed the Cop summit in Antalya, promising “a new era of British leadership” in the struggle against global heating. It’s important to him to talk that way: his political strategy relies on shrinking the appeal of the Green party, whose electoral success earlier this year helped remove his predecessor. But talk only takes you so far. Eventually the words have to be matched by action.



That’s where things get tricky. Last month Burnham’s government approved the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, dismaying climate activists. Soon there will have to be a decision on Rosebank, the much bigger proposed new oilfield northwest of Shetland. There are also signs that ministers are preparing to weaken the targets set for the car industry to shift to electric vehicles. And this week, the chancellor, John Healey, declared himself fully “behind building a third runway at Heathrow”. Small wonder that campaigners are talking of hypocrisy and the government’s “crumbling” credibility.
What is Burnham to do? He has Healey in one ear, telling him that a thriving airport is an engine for economic growth, doubtless alongside the oil, gas and car industries. And in the other he has the climate scientists, reminding him that global carbon emissions are at record levels and the planet is getting hotter every year. What option does he have, except to keep putting off the moment of choice, buying himself time by saying, for example, that Rosebank is a “quasi-legal decision” that cannot be hurried?

‘You cannot build peace on a burning planet,’ UN chief tells Cop31 in farewell speech


António Guterres says climate action central to every aspect of UN’s work, as leaders depart Cop31 and talks go on




Tackling the climate crisis is central to all of human life and must be at the forefront of global governance, the outgoing UN secretary general has said in an emotional farewell address at the Cop31 climate summit.
“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” António Guterres said at his final climate press conference as secretary general on Friday. “You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it. You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends.”

Guterres has been the most forthright secretary general yet on the subject of the climate, returning to it again and again to castigate fossil fuel companies and recalcitrant governments.
He leaves office at the end of December and his successor is still unknown after Donald Trump tried to interject his preferred choices into the process. There are widespread fears that the next incumbent will downplay the climate crisis in favour of other issues.


In a clear message to his successor, Guterres spelled out why the UN must continue to place the climate at the top of the global agenda. “Climate change does not stay in its lane,” he said. “It drives anger and displacement around the world. It wipes out development gains built over decades. It pushes countries deeper into deficit. It aggravates competition for land and water.
“It fuels instability. And increasingly, it threatens the very existence of communities and countries. For all these reasons, I have never viewed climate action as just one of many other issues. Climate action is central to every aspect of the work of the UN.”
Guterres was one of the few world leaders left at Cop by Friday afternoon as most of the more than 90 who had attended returned to their capitals, leaving negotiators to get down to tackling issues such as the electrification of the global economy and a just transition out of fossil fuel industries for workers.

California governor Gavin Newsom endorses global fossil fuel phaseout


Newsom is the most prominent US politician at Cop31, a process the Trump administration continues to boycott




The leader of the world’s fourth biggest economy, California governor Gavin Newsom, has explicitly endorsed a global phase out of the fossil fuels that drive climate breakdown.
Newsom told the Guardian that California is “100%” behind the efforts of the so-called Santa Marta coalition, a group of more than 50 countries that includes many of the world’s largest economies, to transition away from oil, gas and coal toward solar, wind, batteries and other non-carbon energy sources.

Speaking at the Cop31 UN climate summit on Thursday, Newsom said: “When you have a product that is obviously superior, which clean energy is for the climate and the economy, why wouldn’t you make that shift as quickly as possible?”
As the head of America’s most populous and economically powerful state, Newsom is the most prominent US politician at Cop31, a process the administration of US president Donald Trump continues to boycott.






Cop31 as it happened: ‘You cannot build peace on a burning planet’, warns UN chief Guterres in final climate summit speech

Read more
Newsom, a Democrat, is widely expected to run for president in 2028. His statement raises the possibility that the US, the world’s biggest economy and largest historical emitter of planet-warming gases, could join the Santa Marta coalition if he wins the presidency two years from now.
More than 80 countries wanted last year’s COP30 to begin to develop a global “roadmap” to phase out fossil fuels. A handful of petrostates led by Saudi Arabia blocked that effort, relying on the disputed notion that decisions at UN climate summits can only be made by consensus. Undaunted, countries favoring a roadmap met in April in Santa Marta, Colombia, to begin designing a phase out on their own.
“Love it,” Newsom said of the challenge that this Santa Marta “coalition of the willing” is posing to the US and other states intent on keeping the world burning fossil fuels.

The super El Niño is officially here, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center announced Thursday.
Water temperatures in the Pacific Ocean reached the threshold needed for the designation, rising to at least 0.5 of a degree Celsius (0.9 of a degree Fahrenheit) above average for three consecutive months. The natural climate pattern has been in effect since late spring, leading to historic flooding in the southern U.S. and impacting massive ocean swells along coastlines.
But the U.S. hasn’t seen the worst of its impacts yet, with more coming through the spring. 
“El Niño continues to strengthen, with a strong-to-very strong El Niño likely through January-March 2027,” NOAA said.

Full SummaryClimate action for vulnerable nations must include agricultural subsidy reform to ensure a just rural transition, according to Carlos Alvarado. The goal is to redirect the $800 billion spent on global agricultural subsidies toward sustainable practices without undermining food security or farmer livelihoods.
Climate action for the most vulnerable countries cannot be effective without also factoring in agriculture. It is the backbone of many economies and the foundation of food and nutrition security.
The sector is simultaneously among the most important and the most exposed for those on the frontlines of rising temperatures.
And yet many of the most climate-vulnerable countries are also following a similar path set by high-income countries, using public support to inadvertently perpetuate environmentally damaging agricultural practices and inputs, while not supporting smallholder farmers nor guaranteeing nutritious food for people.





As climate negotiators seek to advance the Belem-Antalya Mechanism (BAM) for a just transition at the UN’s Cop31 talks amid a challenging economic context, climate-vulnerable countries must be supported to rethink agricultural subsidies and support to build long-term resilience.
The challenge is not to cut subsidies, but to redirect them without undermining farmers' livelihoods or food security, or in other words, bringing about a just rural transition.

School children are taking part in an event aimed at inspiring climate action, to coincide with the COP31 international climate conference in Turkey.
Hosted at the Kingston Maurwood campus, the first Dorset-wide Youth COP has brought children from 14 schools together to discuss issues including future careers.
Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said young people should be "given a voice" over dealing with climate change.
A Dorset COP 2026 event is also being held on Saturday as world leaders and delegates gather at Antalya in Turkey for the COP31 climate summit.
The Dorset Youth COP event includes discussions about how young people feel about climate change as well as a panel session introducing them to the range of jobs and careers in the climate and energy sectors.
Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said: "Young people are inheriting the climate and ecological emergencies that previous generations have created and need to be given a voice in jointly developing and implementing the solutions to these issues." 
"The Youth COP aims to raise awareness, inspire and support them to take action now and into the future."







More stories from Dorset

The main Dorset COP 2026 event takes place on Saturday also at the Kingston Maurward Campus near Dorchester. 
The fourth annual event brings together community groups, environmental organisations, experts and political leaders.
The programme will explore how Dorset can respond to climate change, nature loss, food resilience, pollution and other environmental challenges.
The programme will also feature an exhibition of over 30 local organisations and a Question Time-style panel bringing together Dorset MPs, council leaders and independent climate experts. 
Giles Watts, chair of Dorset CAN said the event's focus was on making "a lasting positive impact" on climate and nature local areas.
"We want to bring people together, listen to different perspectives and energise local communities and politicians to act more quickly on the pressing challenges we face," he added.

From 36m ago


“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” the UN secretary-general, António Guterres, has warned in a final speech. The outgoing diplomat, and outspoken climate activist, celebrated the progress made in his last decade doing the job while warning of the wide gap between what science demands and politics deliver.
“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” he said. You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it. You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends. And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did least to cause this crisis suffer first and worst.”
Guterres backed the Turkish and Australian co-hosts push for electrification – caveating that it must be clean – and praised the Cop30 presidency’s roadmaps on transitioning away from fossil fuels and on deforestation. He also called for confronting the disproportionate influence of the fossil fuel lobby.
“The future of our planet cannot be negotiated on the terms of those profiting from its destruction.”

Chris Minns has gone out of his way to help ban peaceful protest in Newcastle, the world’s biggest coal port. Voters will remember in March 
 
 




We know that El Niño climate patterns are supercharged by the burning of fossil fuels. In Europe, more than 50,000 people died of intolerable heat this year. And yet, in September the premier of New South Wales, Chris Minns, oversaw the largest coalmine expansion in the state’s history.
Coal from that operation in the Hunter Valley will inevitably increase global warming after it is exported through Newcastle and then burned overseas. Newcastle, the world’s biggest coal port, has become the target of a restless population, particularly of young Australians, alarmed by global warming.

The protest organisers, a group called Rising Tide, are impressive. Their colourful, peaceful and remarkably safe tactics have seen the flow of massive coal-laden ships slowed and sometimes halted as hundreds of kayaks and other craft have formed flotillas in Newcastle’s Hunter River port. As the climate emergency has grown, so have the thousands of people joining Rising Tide’s annual demonstrations.


This week, Minns wrote an endorsement for Newcastle’s lord mayor Gavin Morris’s move to ban protesters from council-owned land. The motion was to prevent any event or protest organised by Rising Tide or associated groups or individuals on council-owned land “now and into the future”. Minns’s letter was used to influence the Morris motion to pass 7-6. Three Greens councillors voted against the motion, while Labor councillors were split. A Liberal councillor said it was an opportunity to rid the city of the “scourge” of Rising Tide. Police were called to settle the ensuing uproar in the council chambers.

View image in fullscreen
An Edwardian home’s bay window being held up by props owing to subsidence in Palmer’s Green, north London. Photograph: EDIFICE/Alamy


UK’s biggest insurer hit by rise in subsidence claims after record hot summer


Increase reported by Aviva after Hastings Direct said claims were up 140% in August and Axa said it had been a ‘surge year’




The UK’s largest insurer has been hit by a rise in subsidence claims after an extremely hot summer left households across the country grappling with the fallout from the growing climate crisis.
Aviva said on Friday it had experienced the jump amid an industry-wide surge in households filing subsidence claims with their insurers to cover repairs, which typically are needed to address cracks, sloping floors, and off-kilter doors and windows.

It follows two record hot summers in the UK; August this year was the joint hottest month ever recorded around the world. Drier summers cause the ground under houses to shrink, which undermines a property’s foundations. It then expands in wetter winters, which can further damage homes.







UK subsidence claims surge after hottest summer on record

Read more
Aviva experienced a “peak subsidence period” between July and September, with claims continuing into October, its chief executive, Amanda Blanc, told Bloomberg in an interview on Friday. Aviva would not provide any further detail on the scale of the increase in claims.
Blanc said homeowners could reduce the risk of subsidence by keeping a close eye on drains, pipes and gutters, and fixing any leaks that could affect the ground under homes. “It’s about managing trees and plumbing,” she said.
A number of fellow insurers have also experienced a rise in claims in recent months. Hastings Direct said it received record subsidence claims in August, up 140% compared with a year earlier. Axa, one of the UK’s biggest home insurers, has said it has been a “surge year” for subsidence.


The value of claims have also hit a record high. The average subsidence claim in the UK hit a high of £20,000 between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers. Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, compared with £60m in the same period last year.
Millions of homes are at risk of subsidence because of the worsening climate crisis, according to the British Geological Survey, which estimates that up to 11% of UK homes – more than 4.2m houses – could be at risk by 2070. Older properties with shallow foundations and those built on clay-rich soil are facing the biggest threat, with areas including London, Essex, Kent and areas around Oxford among the most vulnerable.

More than 100 companies and groups linked to fossil fuels represented at Cop31, study says


Delegations outnumber those of some countries most vulnerable to climate impacts, such as Nepal, which suffered glacier collapse 
 
 
Cop31 live – latest updates  




More than 100 corporations and industry groups linked to fossil fuel interests have sent delegations to the UN climate talks in Turkey, according to an analysis.
The Cop31 climate summit in Antalya is thought to be the largest ever in the three decades of the annual gatherings, with more than 92,000 delegates registered to attend talks aimed at shifting the world away from the fossil fuels that are dangerously overheating our planet.

This swell of people includes numerous groups that support or are influenced by coal, oil and gas interests, the review has found. In total, 103 groups with a track record of obstructing climate action or furthering fossil fuel interests are at Cop31, according to the Kick Big Polluters Out coalition, which comprises about 450 environmental organisations.


The groups include 60 fossil fuel industry bodies, 16 financial companies that fund fossil fuels, six industrial agriculture and foods products groups, three big tech groups and 20 cross-sector organisations.
Among the largest delegations are the International Emissions Trading Association, which has 29 people at Cop and has been accused of helping provide legitimacy to fossil fuel companies, BNP Paribas, HSBC and Amazon. The oil firm Exxon has a delegation of 13 people in Antalya, TotalEnergies has five and BlackRock, another big financier of fossil fuel projects, has five.
These delegations outnumber the national delegations sent by some of the countries most vulnerable to climate impacts. Nepal, which suffered a devastating, deadly glacier collapse this summer that has been linked to global heating, has just a sixth of the number of delegates of these groups.
Prakash Dalal from Pro Public/Friends of the Earth Nepal said: “Big polluters have caused loss of livelihood, emotional damage, trauma and survival challenges for our people.
“We cannot tolerate the disproportionate space given to them compared to civil society and our country delegations.”
Large numbers of fossil fuel lobbyists have long been a feature of the UN climate talks, with one in every 25 participants at last year’s summit in Brazil a fossil fuel lobbyist. Environmental advocates have called for better transparency and conflict of interest disclosures for those attending, and influencing, the climate talks.

A super El Niño brings startling changes for marine life on California coast: ‘like nothing we’ve ever seen’


Water temperatures are climbing the charts, high tides are swallowing the shoreline and vital parts of the food web that feed ocean diversity are disappearing




On a picturesque autumn afternoon last week, the beaches of California’s Monterey Bay were teeming with life and death.
A cadre of shorebirds charged and retreated in a synchronized dance with the raging surf. Nearby, the receding tides had deposited lifeless bundles of feathers and bone, tangled in piles of glistening kelp. Swollen sea lion carcasses, their teeth bared in a quiet grimace, dotted the sand as beach picnickers and dog walkers enjoyed the warm, cloudless day.

The effects of a historic El Niño have officially reached Monterey Bay, according to scientists, and the mortality on display here may be a grim harbinger of more to come. The waters that hug California’s central coast are already undergoing startling changes.


The climate phenomenon, defined by unusually warm equatorial ocean conditions, is rapidly heating and expanding parts of the Pacific. Water temperatures are climbing off the charts, from the ocean’s depths to its surface. Record-smashing high tides are swallowing more of the shoreline. Plus, vital parts of a vibrant food web that feeds ocean diversity are disappearing, starving scores of species throughout the system.


These changes are compounding the impacts from the climate crisis and extreme marine heatwaves that have already stressed ocean ecosystems and their inhabitants.
“It is like nothing we’ve ever seen,” said Dr Jono Wilson, the science director for The Nature Conservancy’s oceans program. “We just are trying to figure out how to wrap our heads around the sheer scale of this event.”
Visual reports from divers, underwater cameras, and beach-goers have showcased how deeply underwater environments are changing. Waters clouded with nutrients cleared as they warmed, and an unusual array of visitors arrived from the southern seas.
The central coast has played host to schools of halfmoon fish that ventured far past their southern California range, translucent winged comb jellyfish generally spotted on dives near Hawaii, and Humboldt squid that are usually found in the eastern equatorial Pacific. Whale sharks common in the Sea of Cortez were seen in Malibu and juvenile garibaldi fish – brilliantly orange speckled with glowing electric blue splotches – were seen for the first time in Monterey Bay.

El Niño stokes a higher risk of death in childbirth for millions of women in the world’s harshest crisis zones, midwives have warned.
Converging waves of weather – floods, cyclones and extreme heat – forecast to peak in the coming months will prove fatal for many, especially pregnant women, who face being cut off from hospital when in labour.

About 15 million babies are due to be born in November and December in countries rated as high risk for El Niño – that represents two in every three births worldwide.
They include Nigeria, Chad, Central African Republic, South Sudan, Somalia and Afghanistan, which already have some of the world’s highest maternal and newborn death rates. About 260,000 women die in pregnancy and childbirth every year, mostly of avoidable causes, with sub-Saharan Africa carrying 70% of the burden.
“If you’re female, pregnant, socially deprived and in a climate catastrophe zone, the odds are stacked against you before you even conceive,” said Anna af Ugglas, chief executive of the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM) today. “El Niño is coming on top of other health risks – and for many this will become the difference between life and death.”


View image in fullscreen
A mother and baby in a clinic in Chad, which has a high maternal and newborn death rate. Photograph: Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images
In Bangladesh, maternity teams are braced for floods.
“Childbirth does not stop during a cyclone, flood, heatwave or landslide,” said Christine Ewoi Eloto, a midwife mentor in the Rohingya refugee camps of Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh. “Even a short delay in reaching a facility during an obstetric emergency can cost a mother or her baby’s life.
“During previous flash floods and landslides, women could not reach health facilities. Roads were submerged and our vehicle got stuck.”
In southern Malawi, a heatwave is keeping women from antenatal care. A failed rainy season has left farming families unable to afford bus fares to a clinic – so issues go untreated.
“At present we’re facing temperatures above 40C most of the week,” said midwife Judith Mgogo. “Antenatal attendance is expected to be low since women cannot travel in such hot weather. We are having electricity blackouts every day.”
When electricity fails, midwives deliver babies in sweltering wards or by torchlight, said midwife Madalitso Ben Malekano, of Phalombe district. “Extreme heat is causing dizziness and fatigue in many women – and that includes myself.”
Previous strong El Niño events have left more than 4 million Malawians short of food. “There will be malnutrition, which will lead to low birthweight babies and heavy maternal bleeding – a consequence of anaemia,” said Ben Malekano.

articles.jina_text:
The UN’s annual climate summit is known for being arcane, long-winded and frustrating. On Wednesday, however, Turkey brought a dash of Eurovision-style glamour to proceedings.
The hosts of the talks, held in the historic Mediterranean city of Antalya, decided to blast assorted world leaders, dignitaries and other delegates with Let’s Cop, a bona fide floor-filler that includes the lines: “Bring down the heat, make it drop. One world, one call, let’s Cop.”

This banger followed a lengthy display of whirling, high-octane dancing by performers in traditional Turkish clothing, and a period of interpretive performance featuring a woman dressed as some sort of shrub and a troupe entangled in a costume formed of plastic waste. But it was Let’s Cop that was the most intriguing.


I’ll tell you why, after today’s climate headlines.
Essential reads
 
 
‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31  
 
Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems  
 
Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow?  
In focus


View image in fullscreen
Dancers of the Fire of Anatolia showcase traditional folk dances. Photograph: Dogukan Keskinkılıç/Anadolu/Getty Images


On hearing Let’s Cop, the immediate, uncharitable, question about this banger was, is this AI? My intrepid colleague Graham Readfearn secured the following answer from the Turkish hosts: “The song’s melody and lyrics were written by a professional musician, while AI tools were used in the composition and production process.”
Whatever that cryptic explanation means, the shades of Eurovision introduced by Let’s Cop were a welcome fillip for a climate conference that has been bedevilled by troubled logistics and a distinct lack of progress – or even direction – on the central priorities of ending the fossil-fuel era and adequately supporting the countries most vulnerable to climate disasters.
There is still a long way to go in Cop31, which is slated to finish next Friday. But so far, to extend the metaphor: what would the Eurovision-style scores be?
Well, Turkey and Australia jointly oversee this Cop and yet each are significant consumers of fossil fuels and are actively increasing their polluting activities even as the climate conference is under way? Nul points.
Countries are cutting their emissions far too slowly to avoid disastrous climate breakdown and yet talk of ending fossil fuels is still considered a bit too risque? Nul points.

World is now in ‘age of electricity’, energy agency chief says


Exclusive: Fossil fuels no longer dominant energy source, IEA leader says, as summit considers electrification pledge




The world has left behind the age of coal, oil and gas and is now firmly in “the age of electricity”, the world’s leading energy economist has said.
Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), said more than twice as much electricity generation would be added to the global economy in the next decade than in the last, as countries scramble to secure their energy supplies against fossil fuel price volatility and supply shocks, such as the Iran war.

Transport is being electrified at an unprecedented rate: outside China, sales of electric cars have risen by 60% in the last nine months, the IEA has found. The growth of AI datacentres is also spurring electricity generation, as is the rapid growth in air conditioning, according to Birol, as heatwaves grow more intense and more frequent under rising global temperatures.







The planet ‘is being killed’, Greta Thunberg tells Cop31 climate summit

Read more
“We will still use oil and gas, but the dominant source of energy is becoming electricity,” Birol told the Guardian in an interview at the Cop31 UN climate summit in Turkey. “One staggering number [is that] in the last 10 years, the world has added about 5,000 gigawatts of electricity. And we expect, in a very conservative way, in the next 10 years, about 12,000 gigawatts, more than two times more than what we had in the last 10 years.”
Governments from 185 countries are meeting this week and next in Antalya for the annual talks, where the turn to electrification in place of fossil fuels is one of the key topics. A resolution to derive 35% of final energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 is on the table, which if it succeeds, could be one of the most important ways of achieving the needed decarbonisation of economies by mid-century.
Electricity now fulfils about a quarter of most energy needs while three-quarters of final energy worldwide is supplied by fossil fuels, mostly for transport, heating and industrial uses. Global electricity was increasingly generated by renewable sources and that process would speed up even faster over the next decades, Birol said.


View image in fullscreen
Fatih Birol at the Cop31 summit on Thursday. Photograph: Adem Kutucu/Anadolu/Getty Images

articles.jina_text:
Owning an electric car, driving an electric motorbike taxi, riding scooters – we speak to people in Oslo, Kigali and Shanghai about their everyday routines




The race to electrification has emerged as a key theme of this year’s UN climate summit: increasing the use of electricity – particularly from clean sources – has the potential to improve daily life for people around the world.
The summit’s co-hosts are now trying to get countries to promise to increase their electricity use to 35% of all energy used by 2035. The global figure currently stands at 23%, but some countries are already striding ahead. As 100,000 delegates, negotiators and world leaders thrash out the details in Antalya, Turkey, the Guardian spoke to three people in Norway, Rwanda and China to find out what life looks like in more highly electrified countries.

An office worker in Oslo, Norway


View image in fullscreen
‘I mostly use my electric car on weekends,’ says Unni Berge, who lives in ‘a rather energy-efficient flat’ in Oslo with her husband and two sons. Photograph: Norwegian EV Association
Norway is a world leader in the race to 100% electrification. In September, a record 98.81% of new cars sold were electric, and hydropower produces 90% of all electricity. But with rapidly rising energy demands, including from new datacentres, authorities warn that the country could soon face a power deficit and higher energy prices.


Unni Berge, 47, lives in Oslo with her husband and two teenage sons and works as the head of communications at the Norwegian EV Association. She describes how electricity features in a typical day:
“I use electricity in my three-bedroom flat and I have district heating [where heat is transported around a local network from a centralised source rather than individual boilers to heat homes and buildings]. For electricity we are connected to the Norwegian central grid, which is mainly hydropower.
“I live in a rather energy-efficient flat, so our electricity bills are comparatively low. In October, we spent 730 Norwegian kroner [£57] on electricity for our apartment, and in September it was 500 kroner.


View image in fullscreen
Electric cars charging at a station in Alta, in Finnmark, northern Norway. Nearly 99% of new cars sold in Norway in September were electric.  Photograph: Salwan Georges/Washington Post/Getty Images


“I go to work by bus. Almost all the buses in Oslo are fully electric. I also have an electric car, but driving in the middle of Oslo for work is not an option because we have a lot of restrictions on cars in the city centre. In my street, the bus comes every fifth minute, so I don’t have to plan. I go outside and a bus comes.
“I mostly use my electric car on weekends. A lot of the trips are driving to sports activities with my two children, who are 18 and 15. I also train a handball team, so I use it to go to a lot of handball matches and tournaments.
