articles.title: How much air pollution is in your London area? Interactive map gives real-time level amid weather alert
articles.raw_rss: Much of the capital had an ‘unhealthy’ rating for air pollution earlier this week
articles.raw_meta: Much of the capital had an ‘unhealthy’ rating for air pollution earlier this week
articles.jina_text:
Londoners have been warned of dangerously high levels of air pollution this week, with online data showing that levels could result in “serious health effects”.




Periods of dense fog combined with low wind allowed harmful particles to build up across the capital, with a high air pollution alert in effect in London on Tuesday on advice from forecasters at Imperial College London.








Vulnerable residents in particular were urged to take care, in the fourth high air pollution alert issued by Mayor Sadiq Khan so far this year.




Forecasters say that smoke from Bonfire Night and Diwali fireworks, as well as wood burning, are likely to have contributed to the high levels.


Fog shrouding the London Eye
AFP/Getty




Since Tuesday, levels have fallen across the capital - but some parts of London still have levels which could cause moderate health concerns for people who are unusually sensitive to air pollution. 




An interactive map, created by the World Air Quality Index Project, is a real-time source of air quality information across the city. 




The site, which covers major cities around the world, collates data from more than half a million air quality monitoring stations across the planet, in a bid to raise awareness of air pollution.











According to the site’s data, between Sunday and Tuesday, much of the capital was in the “unhealthy” zone - meaning everyone could begin to experience health effects, and members of sensitive groups could experience more serious health effects.




The site suggests that active children and adults, and people with respiratory disease, should avoid prolonged outdoor exertion during such conditions.


Air Quality Index scores recorded in London this week
World Air Quality Index Project,


Much of London was in the 'unhealthy' zone earlier this week
World Air Quality Index Project,




Some London boroughs were covered by the highest levels of pollution, according to air pollution maps provided by the Apple Weather app. 







The City of Westminster, Wandsworth, Lambeth, Merton, Ealing, Brent, Tower Hamlets, Greenwich and Bexley were all rated 10 earlier this week, with most of the other boroughs being rated 8 or 6, including Croydon, Richmond upon Thames and Kensington and Chelsea.




North London had somewhat clearer air, according to the maps, with boroughs including Haringey and Enfield mainly being rated 2 or 4. 


A map of air pollution in London from earlier this week
Apple Weather




Particularly foggy conditions caused disruptions at London's airports on Monday, with several flights from Heathrow and London City airports cancelled.

articles.title: COP31: Burnham announces appointment of world’s first special representative for climate security
articles.raw_rss: Before Andy Burnham travelled to Dublin for a meeting of the European Political Community, he started the day in Turkey.
articles.raw_content:
Before Andy Burnham travelled to Dublin for a meeting of the European Political Community, he started the day in Turkey.
The Prime Minister told the COP31 conference that climate change was a matter of national security.
He said that this summer, which saw multiple wildfires, droughts and heatwaves, “was not normal”’
In a world first, he also announced he had appointed a former Chair of the Joint Intelligence Committee as a new Special Representative for Climate Security.

That’s all for today. Here are the highlights of the fourth day of the 31st UN climate summit:
 
 
“Britain is back and ready to play its part,” UK prime minister Andy Burnham said in a speech that was criticised at home for a lack of action to back it up.  
 
Earth is on track for ‘irrecoverable overshoot’ of 1.5C target, scientists announced, with 2.7C of heating expected by the end of the century.  
 
Leaders from several poor and low-emitting countries urged rich polluters to stump up more cash and demanding emissions cuts that keep overshoot low and short.  
 
Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate activist, said the planet is “not dying, it is being killed, and we know by who.”  
 
John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, called president Donald Trump the “biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time” for scrapping action on the climate crisis and ceding the clean energy race to China.  
 
Polluting companies have sued governments for nearly half a trillion dollars in secret courts, an analysis found.  
Thanks for following – we’ll be back tomorrow morning with more.

articles.jina_text:
An indigenous climate activist who is taking the Australian government to the UN human rights committee over its coal and gas exports stood alongside Greta Thunberg at Cop summit to demand Anthony Albanese “stop speaking and start listening.”
Draped in traditional dress in front of a media throng, Rikki Dank, a Gudanji and Wakaya traditional owner, delivered an impassioned plea to Albanese to listen to “the Australian people when they say no more new coal, oil and gas”.







‘I was home alone when the glacier collapsed. My mum called and told me to run’ – This is climate breakdown

Read more
Albanese on Thursday defended his major speech at the opening of Cop31 after facing criticism for omitting the phrase “fossil fuels”.
Australia is the president of the two-week negotiations at Cop31 being held in Antalya, Turkey. A key push from the two hosts is to garner support for a “35 by 35” pledge for 35% of end-use energy to be from electricity by the year 2035.
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, and several countries are pushing the two hosts to also progress a proposal from last year’s Cop president, Brazil, to have countries develop roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels.
Squeezed into a corner of the vast Cop31 media centre, Thunberg was flanked by Dank and other climate advocates, including a Nepalese MP who had helped rescue people from a landslide that followed an August glacier collapse that killed more than 1,500 people.
Thunberg said: “It is more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be less under control. The planet is not dying, it is being killed.






Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?

Read more
“And we know by who. And it is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue.”
She said it was “common sense” that Australia needed to take greater action on climate change.
Dank is one of 10 Australians behind a complaint before the UN human rights committee – known as the Hard Truths case – that claims the Australian government has failed to protect them from climate pollution, including from its vast exports of coal and LNG that are among the highest in the world.
Lawyers behind the case are hoping for a resolution in the next 18 months. While a committee declaration is not legally binding, a negative finding would be a major embarrassment and would carry significant political weight.
“My Country is being fracked, our drinking water poisoned and our history erased as we speak,” said Dank.
She said the prime minister “needs to stop speaking and start listening to our brothers and sisters across the world when they say they don’t want us to export coal, oil or gas and the climate harms that they bring with them”.
Albanese had a series of bi-lateral meetings on the sidelines of Cop31 on Thursday with Bangladesh, Lebanon, Pacific leaders and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.

articles.title: Shortages of antibiotics and ADHD drugs set to be eased under new Brexit deal
articles.raw_rss: UK and EU will share information on how to best source medicine supplies
articles.raw_content:
The UK and EU are set to strike a deal to help tackle post-Brexit shortages of medicines such as antibiotics, ADHD medication and epilepsy drugs at next week’s reset summit.



The two sides are finalising a health security agreement that will help address shortages of certain drugs which have got worse since Brexit, according to a draft text of a joint UK-EU statement seen by The i Paper.



The deal is designed to boost the sharing of intelligence on medicine supplies, helping the two sides collaborate as they experience supply shortages driven by global instability, but also partly by post-Brexit trade barriers in the case of the UK.



Experts on post-Brexit health policy said the planned deal appeared to be “significant” and a “good first step” in addressing shortages that have hit both sides of the Channel in recent years, with recent crises in obtaining medicines such antibiotics needed for winter illnesses, and critical products to help people with long-term conditions such as ADHD and epilepsy.



It is expected to come alongside a major Brexit reset package of agreements on food and drink trade, carbon markets and youth mobility that Andy Burnham said will boost the UK’s economy by adding 0.4 per cent to gross domestic product.



An EU draft text of a joint statement, which is forming a key part of the negotiations, refers to both sides using the 20 November summit in Brussels to welcome the signing of a memorandum of understanding on health security.

The deal is designed to boost the sharing of intelligence on medicine supplies, helping the two sides collaborate as they experience supply shortages driven by global instability, but also partly by post-Brexit trade barriers in the case of the UK.



 
Experts on post-Brexit health policy said the planned deal appeared to be “significant” and a “good first step” in addressing shortages that have hit both sides of the Channel in recent years, with recent crises in obtaining medicines such antibiotics needed for winter illnesses, and critical products to help people with long-term conditions such as ADHD and epilepsy. 
It is expected to come alongside a major Brexit reset package of agreements on food and drink trade, carbon markets and youth mobility that Andy Burnham said will boost the UK’s economy by adding 0.4 per cent to gross domestic product. 
An EU draft text of a joint statement, which is forming a key part of the negotiations, refers to both sides using the 20 November summit in Brussels to welcome the signing of a memorandum of understanding on health security. 
Deal is ‘significant’ 
This will include “matters concerning medical countermeasures” and the finalisation of a specialised committee on health security as part of the overarching post-Brexit trade deal.



 
The i Paper has learnt this will help both sides inform each other of where there are shortages and share information on how to source supplies. 
Mark Dayan, Brexit programme lead at the Nuffield Trust, a health think-tank, said the deal was “significant” and would help both the UK and EU, which have been dealing with a “really bad four or five years for medicines shortages… a really serious issue that is affecting patient care and taking up a huge amount of pharmacists’ time in the NHS”. 
“Because of the way managing medicine shortages works, finding out about them sooner is really useful,” he said. 
“It should allow the UK and EU to have better intelligence, and that they are able to identify better where there are stocks and move them around. 
“Those are things that are very important with how you respond to an individual medicine shortage and try to make sure it never reaches patients.” 
It comes with the UK facing extra barriers to bringing medicines to the country and moving them the other way to the EU due to extra regulatory steps and border checks necessitated by Brexit.

Full SummaryClimate activist Greta Thunberg criticized wealthy governments at the Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, claiming they are failing to address the climate crisis. Leaders from Mali, Seychelles, and Palau also called for urgent action as nations at the frontline of the crisis face existential threats.
Climate activist Greta Thunberg has hit out at wealthy governments for not taking the climate crisis seriously enough, saying that the planet is “not dying, it is being killed and we know by who”. 
Speaking amid a throng of press on the sidelines of the UN’s Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey – the first time she has attended the conference in five years – she said that it is “being killed by the very same people thought to come to our rescue.” 
“No one is coming to our rescue... When our human rights are being threatened by states and other institutions, it’s our duty to stand up and be the adult in the room and fight for everyone’s human rights,” she added. 





The conference comes in a year marked by destructive weather events, including lethal floods and heatwaves, alongside energy market turbulence triggered by the Iran war.
It comes as nations at the frontline of the climate crisis – facing an existential threat – have called on larger countries to act now, as there is zero time to waste.

articles.title: Clean-up begins as oil spill shuts 18 Kent beaches
articles.raw_rss: The source of the oil, which has closed beaches in Ramsgate and Margate, has not been identified.
articles.raw_meta: The source of the oil, which has closed beaches in Ramsgate and Margate, has not been identified.
articles.jina_text:
Eighteen beaches in Kent have been closed due to an oil spill which the local council said will take "many days" to clean-up.
"Significant deposits of oil" were found at beaches across the Isle of Thanet, including Ramsgate and the popular tourist beaches of Margate and Broadstairs.
Thanet District Council (TDC) reported the incident on Wednesday evening and the Environmental Agency (EA) is investigating. The source of the oil has not been identified.
Mike Humber, director for the environment at the council, told BBC South East: "We never want to be saying to the public to not go on the beaches, but we have taken that decision to protect the public."
He added: "We want to clean up as quickly as we can. I think it will be many days, but it's difficult to be sure on that kind of timescale.

Mr Burnham, whose jet has also flown around 1,000 miles within the UK, is close to being able to circle the world after touching down in Dublin for today's European Political Community summit.

However, Mr Burnham's taxpayer-funded jet is estimated to have pumped out around 300 tonnes of CO2 since he took office.


The figure, based on the jet burning around 2,200kg of fuel an hour and each kilogram releasing just over three kilograms of CO2, is around 70 times the 4.53 tonnes the average Briton produces in a year.

Full SummaryForeign Secretary Ed Miliband described billions in pledges for the Tropical Forest Forever Facility as a powerful signal of global momentum to protect forests. The initiative, which pays countries to conserve standing forest, has received support from both wealthy donors and developing nations like Indonesia and Brazil.
Billions of dollars in pledges for a high-profile forest protection fund from developing countries – and not just a small group of traditional donors with dwindling aid budgets – represents a ”powerful signal” of aid efforts to help the climate crisis, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has suggested. 
Mr Miliband made the comments to The Independent after a high profile event at Cop31 where countries reaffirmed commitments to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF): a new forest finance initiative designed to pay tropical forest countries a recurring, performance-based amount per hectare of conserved standing forest.
Launched by President Lula at Cop30 in Brazil last year, the fund has now been promised £400m from the UK, $500m (£380m) from the Netherlands, and nearly $100m from climate philanthropies. 




Norway has promised to fund up to 20 per cent of the facility's initial $10 billion capitalisation target, and it is to receive $1bn from Indonesia and $1bn from Brazil: two rainforest nations that are also developing countries, and therefore do not typically face the same expectations as wealthier Western nations to provide aid
Speaking to The Independent after a period of sweeping aid cuts from developed countries including the UK, Mr Miliband commended the fact that a broader group of nations was supporting the fund.

Downing Street has defended Andy Burnham’s attendance at the Cop31 summit on a trip across two countries amid questions about whether the journey delivered value for money and reflected his net-zero ambitions.




No 10 said flying to Turkey for the climate conference and then to Ireland for the European Political Community (EPC) meeting was “absolutely” a good use of the Prime Minister’s time.








Scrutiny of Mr Burnham’s travel has heightened after a Government plane was flown from London to Manchester to pick him up on the way to a Commonwealth summit in the Caribbean last week, earning him the nickname Air Miles Andy among opponents.




Andy Burnham has said the UK is committed to meeting its 2050 net zero target and working with other countries to reach theirs.




The Prime Minister has so far made four international trips since entering office in July, to show support for Ukraine, to attend the UN general assembly in the US, to sign a defence treaty in Germany and his most recent to Antigua.




By the end of Thursday he will have visited two more countries – Turkey for the UN’s Cop31 gathering, where he delivered a five-minute speech pledging a “new era” of British leadership on the green transition, and Ireland for the EPC.

“He said that the climate crisis is not a distant threat; it is upon us all now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere.




“As the Prime Minister said in his speech this morning, climate leadership and action have become more urgent, and Britain will answer the call.”








Pressed on whether that meant No 10 thought it was a good use of time, she said: “Absolutely.”

Addressing other world leaders and delegates at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, he said that despite this, the UK was ready to begin a "new era of British leadership" on the climate change issue.
But environmental campaigners at the summit said the PM had to back up his warm words with stronger actions.
In recent months, the UK government has announced policies which critics say have weakened its green credentials, such as reducing support for heat pumps, approving the Jackdaw gas field and doubling down on support for Heathrow Airport's expansion.
Burnham opened his speech on Thursday by talking about the heat experienced in the UK this past summer.
He said "it was not normal" - in fact it was the hottest on record, made 130 times more likely because of climate change, according to the Met Office.
Hundreds of schools were closed, cereal harvests were down 11%, and ambulance services were inundated with calls beyond levels seen during the Covid-19 pandemic.

As a result this was "placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world", she added.

The current president is the US, which has been a notable absentee from the COP process over the last two years since President Trump withdrew the country from the most important global climate treaty - the Paris Climate Agreement.

articles.jina_text:
A cluster of candy cane-striped smoke stacks dots the horizon of Tufts Cove in Nova Scotia, Canada. Deep in the briny depths of Halifax harbour, something huge is happening: the ocean is being engineered to remove atmospheric carbon.
“This is what Mother Nature has done naturally for a few billion years in order to rebalance the atmospheric and ocean chemistry over long timescales,” says Dr Greg Rau, co-founder and senior scientist at Planetary Technologies.

Planetary Technologies is an ocean carbon-removal firm and one of a growing number of companies attempting to decrease excess atmospheric carbon – the main driver of the climate crisis – by speeding up naturally occurring carbon cycles in the ocean.
To do this, the company conducts ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE), adding a chalk-like substance to the seawater, which allows the water to absorb and store more atmospheric carbon than usual.

Ocean alkalinity enhancement works by dissolving alkaline minerals to increase the seawater’s pH, which leads to carbon dioxide being drawn down into the ocean
This process also helps to offset ocean acidification, often called the “evil twin” of the climate crisis, which is increasing dramatically.
Because it relies on an already occurring process, proponents say these technologies will not harm the marine creatures that call this harbour home, such as mackerel, sunfish, harbour seals and sea turtles. But some marine scientists worry that adding any extra materials to an already stressed ecosystem might harm aquatic life and say that this field of marine geoengineering needs more research.
“If we develop a new medicine, you have steps that you’re supposed to take. You don’t just find a substance and just implement it,” says Sam Dupont, a senior lecturer at the University of Gothenburg. “And at the moment, with [ocean carbon removal] it seems you’re jumping to clinical trial immediately.”
Planetary Technologies runs its operations five days a week. Working out of a shipping container, it adds an alkaline slurry, its proprietary formula, to a local power company’s cooling water to create an odourless milky composite, which is then discharged into Halifax harbour and monitored by their sensors.
Bolstered initially by small government grants, venture funds and other private capital, Planetary Technologies now generates revenue by selling carbon-removal credits worth millions of dollars to companies such as JPMorgan Chase and Shopify.
Ocean carbon removal is a fledgling industry but one that has seen more than $500m (£370m) invested since 2021, according to Ocean Carbon Removal Watch, a database launched by the Pulitzer Center, which tracks marine carbon dioxide removal (mCDR) investments.

articles.title: Burnham commits to 2050 net zero target and working with others to reach theirs

Andy Burnham has said “Britain is back and ready to play its full part” in tackling climate change in a “new era” of leadership over the next decade as he addressed the UN Cop31 summit in Turkey.




Amid accusations that his Government is deprioritising the green agenda, the Prime Minister recommitted to hitting its 2050 net zero target and to working with other countries to reach theirs.








Attending the annual climate gathering for the first time as Prime Minister on Thursday, he warned that the “climate crisis is upon all of us now” after a “not normal” summer of extreme heat, wildfires and drought.




“The climate crisis is not a distant threat; it is upon us all now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere,” he said.




Andy Burnham has said the UK is committed to meeting its 2050 net zero target and working with other countries to reach theirs.




“Meanwhile, two wars across two continents have sent fuel prices and gas bills soaring for families and businesses across the world. The common thread running through all of this: our dependence on fossil fuels.




“The message I carry here at my first Cop as UK Prime Minister is this: we’re committed to meeting our 2050 net zero target, and committed to working with all of our partners to reach theirs.”




Mr Burnham is expected to be the only G7 leader to address the summit in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, with US President Donald Trump declining to send a delegation for the second year running.












He was the first speaker at the conference on Thursday, addressing a half-empty plenary hall at the start of the session with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and London Mayor Lord Sadiq Khan in the audience.




“Britain will live up to its commitments. We will help our friends as they live up to theirs. Britain is back and ready to play its full part,” Mr Burnham said.








As the world will overshoot 1.5C warming above pre-industrial levels this century – a central target of the Paris Agreement – “climate leadership and action have become more urgent”, the Labour leader said.




“Britain will answer the call. Climate is a national security issue.”




As part of these efforts, Dame Madeleine Alessandri, former chairwoman of the Joint Intelligence Committee which provides ministers with national security assessments, has been appointed special representative for climate security, the Prime Minister said.


Andy Burnham told the conference that Britain is ready ‘to play its full part’ (Stefan Rousseau/PA)

Calling on industry leaders to “play their part” to help people on all incomes make the green transition, Mr Burnham said: “This crisis can only be solved in partnership. I have pledged a new era of British leadership over the next decade.

articles.title: 'Summer was a wake-up call, winter could be dire' warning over food supplies
articles.raw_rss: Wales needs to grow more fruit and veg or it will be at the mercy of wars and climate change, one expert says.
articles.raw_meta: Wales needs to grow more fruit and veg or it will be at the mercy of wars and climate change, one expert says.
articles.jina_text:
Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call, and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.
The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.
It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this. 
Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust, external, which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets.
Despite 90% of the country being used for agriculture, external, only about 0.1% is currently being used for horticulture, external.
Growers at Fisher's Wern Farm, near Newtown, Powys, said this must change if the country is to survive climate change, wars and other global disruptions to the supply chain.
"We are hugely dependent and these vegetables are coming from really vulnerable parts of the world like south Europe and north Africa - the areas most prone to drought, fires and overheating," said Fisher.
Food security has become a hot topic, with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying in October people should have water, tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.
Fisher referenced this appeal, adding the UK "has an incredibly centralised food system with 95% of the food we eat bought from nine supermarkets".
He said: "There's no storage, it's a just-in-time system so the food is stored in lorries moving across motorways.
"That is a security hazard because it's very vulnerable to cyber-attacks.
"If the system goes wrong, there's no resilience in it. The food just runs out straight away."




Image source, Duncan Fisher
Image caption, 

Duncan Fisher said he has hope that Wales will be able to increase its fruit and veg growing




Fisher and Sue Holbrook launched Our Food Trust about 10 years ago with the aim of growing more produce locally for local markets.
They found one of the main barriers was stable housing for farmers.
As Fisher explained: "If there's a high wind during the night, they need to get out there and protect things.
"If a sheep gets in, they have to get the sheep out before the entire thing is destroyed in an hour. So they have to live there."
But he said planning regulations have made it really difficult to build homes on farmland.
However, by working with Powys council and Bannau Brycheiniog National Park Authority, they have been able to build three temporary homes for farmers on 36 acres of council-owned land.
They are currently building three more.




Image source, Lydia Dibben
Image caption, 

Lydia Dibben, one of the growers, said even though it was a difficult year they were able to grow a lot of food




One of the growers at Wern Farm is Lydia Dibben, 28, and she agreed access to land is one of the biggest barriers to new farmers.

World heading for ‘irrevocable overshoot’ of global temperature thresholds, analysis warns


Failure to cut emissions will ‘consign humanity to disasters they are unable to adapt to’, report says




The world is heading for an “irrecoverable overshoot” of global temperature thresholds that will plunge billions of people into disastrous climate impacts because governments have stalled for so long to cut planet-heating emissions, analysis has found.
Under current policies, the planet will heat up by 2.7C on average by the end of the century compared with preindustrial times, the report by Climate Action Tracker (CAT) found. This is up slightly from a prediction of 2.6C in the group’s analysis conducted last year.

This level of warming smashes the 1.5C threshold that was agreed by countries a decade ago but is set to be breached in just a few years. Scientists have warned that beyond this point already harmful storms, droughts, heatwaves, flooding and other impacts will become intolerable for parts of the world and potentially trigger runaway climate change that won’t be contained.







‘My classroom was 30C. No one was learning. Then I started to feel dizzy’ – This is climate breakdown

Read more
Countries, minus the US, are gathered in the Turkish city of Antalya for UN climate talks that have centred on the looming “overshoot” of the temperature target. This reality should compel governments to act quickly to phase out use of the fossil fuels that are causing the climate crisis, the UN secretarygeneral, António Guterres, said on Tuesday.
If countries did act decisively to slash emissions then the future temperature projections would become less daunting, the CAT report states. However, in even the most optimistic scenario – where all pledges, targets and other long-term promises made by countries were fulfilled – the world would still heat up by 1.9C by the end of the century.
Such targets have been routinely flouted by the countries that have made them, however. This means leaders face a crunch moment, experts say.


“The stark choice for governments is to either continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to – or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever,” says Bill Hare, chief executive of CAT partner organisation Climate Analytics.

articles.title: We can save more endangered species, says William at conservation awards
articles.raw_rss: The prince met celebrity supporters of African wildlife conservation charity Tusk including comedian John Bishop and ex-footballer Mathieu Flamini.
articles.raw_meta: The prince met celebrity supporters of African wildlife conservation charity Tusk including comedian John Bishop and ex-footballer Mathieu Flamini.
articles.jina_text:
The prince met celebrity supporters of African wildlife conservation charity Tusk including comedian John Bishop and ex-footballer Mathieu Flamini.

        







The Prince of Wales delivers a speech at the 14th annual Tusk Conservation Award(Aaron Chown/PA)
PA Wire

Sam Hall
16 hours ago







The Prince of Wales has said more endangered species can be saved despite conservation being “hard and often dangerous”, as he presented awards for African wildlife protection.





William attended the Tusk Conservation Awards on Wednesday evening, celebrating those on the front line protecting Africa’s wildlife, wild places and communities.




The prince is the royal patron of African wildlife conservation charity Tusk and helped to launch the first awards in 2013.




The Prince of Wales has said more endangered species can be saved despite conservation being “hard and often dangerous”, as he presented awards for African wildlife protection.




He met celebrity supporters including comedian John Bishop and former Arsenal footballer Mathieu Flamini after arriving at the ceremony at five-star hotel Raffles London at the Old War Office.




Since 2011, at least 565 African rangers have been killed in the line of duty, while only 50% of rangers have access to insurance and only 40% have adequate health and safety training.








William, dressed in black tie with a poppy attached, told the audience the “challenges facing our natural world have evolved dramatically” since the Tusk awards began 13 years ago.




He added that “we cannot forget that those who are among the most impacted by our changing climate are also at the forefront of protecting it” and “too many rangers pay the ultimate price on the front line of conservation”.




Discussing the award winners, the prince said: “May their achievements inspire us all to build on this momentum and go further.




“To believe that we can save more endangered species. That we can restore threatened habitats.”




William added: “Those working on the front lines of conservation are now contending not just with the illegal wildlife trade, but the growing impacts of climate change, biodiversity loss, and its ripple effects on the ecosystems and communities that depend on them.













“This has demanded new approaches, adaptability and an extraordinary capacity for innovation in the face of increasingly complex challenges.”




He said: “We know conservation works. In Africa, the mountain gorilla population is on an upward trend. Black rhino numbers are increasing in Kenya, and in southern Africa, elephant populations are also recovering.









“But we know that conservation is hard and often dangerous. While significant strides are being made, organised crime continues to exploit and traffic protected wildlife.




“We must be on continual guard to ensure our endangered species are protected, and that hard-won progress is not reversed.”

UK appoints world’s first special representative for climate security


Exclusive: Madeleine Alessandri, former chair of joint intelligence committee, will take on role of advising No 10 on climate-related national security risks




The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.
Prime minister Andy Burnham will announce the move on Thursday at Cop31, the UN climate summit, with the new role designed to advise the government on national security risks from the climate crisis before they spell catastrophe.

Burnham will tell the key climate talks on Thursday morning: “We should all recognise the summer was not normal. The climate crisis is upon all of us now. We saw that with the wildfires that devastated lives and livelihoods everywhere.”
This year’s summer was the UK’s hottest on record, with back-to-back heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis causing health services and transport to suffer, schools to close and thousands of people to lose their lives prematurely.


Burnham will add: “The message I carry here, in my first Cop as prime minister, is that the UK remains determined to reach net zero by 2050 and to work with our partners to build a clean energy future. The world has changed. The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate action has broken down. 
 
 “We will not stand by, and that’s why I’ve pledged a new era of British leadership over the next decade.”


View image in fullscreen
UK climate group Mothers Rise Up protest near Downing Street in September to highlight the impact of record-breaking heat on children. Photograph: Adrian Dennis/AFP/Getty Images


Burnham arrived in Antalya, Turkey late on Wednesday night, before joining scores of heads of state and government for a series of high-level meetings at the talks, which are presided over jointly by Turkey and Australia. He will also confirm UK support for a proposed target of 35% electrification by 2035 and help towards plans to raise £5bn in private finance for clean energy projects across the world.
Madeleine Alessandri, the former chair of the UK’s joint intelligence committee (JIC), which oversees MI5 and MI6, will take on the special representative job.
But campaigners pointed to what they said were Burnham’s failures to take the measures needed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions at home, and to provide the funding needed to protect vulnerable countries overseas from the kind of risks the JIC has warned about. ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31


Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for a windfall tax on oil and gas firms




Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit.
Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals.

She described seeing bright, lush coral beneath the water of her home island in July that had been bleached white just months later.
“It’s time to wake up,” said Heine. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”



Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement.
“The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up.
“Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”


View image in fullscreen
Hilda Heine giving her speech at the Cop31 leaders’ summit, in which she told delegates: ‘It’s time to wake up.’ Photograph: Mehmet Emin Menguarslan/Anadolu/Getty Images


The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.

His speech – a salvo aimed at boosting the talks – was one of the last Guterres, a vocal climate advocate, will deliver as secretary general before he stands down next month.
“We need an extraordinary acceleration,” Guterres said. “Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”

Full SummaryUK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will address the Cop31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, arguing that the climate crisis is a major threat to national security. He intends to highlight how climate breakdown leads to food insecurity, economic disruption, and migration, while calling for increased investment in clean energy and urgent methane cuts.
The national security of every country is at risk from the climate crisis, the UK's foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will tell world leaders at the Cop31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.
Mr Miliband will say that security and defence objectives are the new "frontier" of climate action, because the rapid heating of the planet will bring food shortages, economic disruption, migration and conflict. 
"National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action; the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news," he told the Guardian before his speech.




He said the climate crisis was among the biggest threats to national security. 
"We should be clear that climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face," Mr Miliband said. "Food security, threats to infrastructure, and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis]," he added.

Guterres launches into a plea for accelerated action to cut emissions and takes direct aim at the fossil fuel industry. The UN chief has already called on countries to push forward a phase out of fossil fuels, rather than merely hinting at it, here at Cop.


UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres makes his plea to the leaders summit at Cop31. Photograph: Dogukan Keskinkilic/Anadolu/Getty Images
“The case for fossil fuels is collapsing,” he said. “Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs. And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do.”
“It’s time to kick the habit – and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said. Guterres likes a good pun and one of his final climate speeches has a decent one: “It’s make or bake time.”

She’s followed by Nikos Christodoulides, president of Cyprus, who has touted his nation’s role in helping the wider Mediterranean and Middle East region. He has also warned against divisions in our fight against global warming. “Climate change transcends politics and does not recognise borders.”


As you may be sick of hearing from me already on this blog, I think the Cop31 theme tune “Let’s Cop” is a bit of a catchy banger.
“Bring down the heat make it drop.” 
 “One world, one call, let’s Cop.”
But there may be a cruel twist that might quell my enthusiasm. First, have a listen.



The Cop31 theme song, “Let’s Cop”.
One of my Australian reporter colleagues here spent many years as a tech reporter and thought she smelt the whiff of AI. More than one AI detector, she said, suggested she might be right.
So I asked the Turkish hosts if “Let’s Cop” might be AI slop (this isn’t exactly how I put it and, to be fair, I don’t think it is slop but the rhyme as too good to resist). Here’s what they said:
“The song’s lyrics and composition were created by a professional artist, with AI technology used solely to assist with the vocals.”
Did that mean the singing voice and the instruments were AI?
“The song’s melody and lyrics was written by a professional musician, while AI tools were used in the composition and production process.”
Make of that what you will. I now hate that I like it.

By emphasizing the direct impacts of extreme heat on communities and families, campaigners hope to drive greater government accountability and public advocacy.

The country faced an estimated 642.9 million working hours lost in 2024 due to heat stress, according to the Cop presidency – while a record temperature of 50.5C recorded in 2025 coincided with devastating wildfires that burned some 154,000 hectares.

articles.jina_text:
Anthony Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on climate change in a historic speech to the UN’s climate summit, but one which failed to mention the fossil fuels driving the crisis.
The Australia prime minister landed in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya on Wednesday morning where the Cop31 talks are being presided over by his climate change minister, Chris Bowen, but hosted by Turkey.







Developing countries in limbo as rich nations delay new climate finance plans

Read more
Only moments before Albanese spoke, on the same stage the UN secretary general Antonio Guterres said unambiguously that keeping the 1.5C temperature goal alive “means no new coal”.
In a packed conference room, Turkey put on an opening ceremony of whirling traditional dancers, booming music and a film shot around the world with characters saying “We need to talk”.
“This is an historic moment for my country,” said Albanese, adding Australia was “proud to be a leader on climate action.”
“Proud to be a renewable energy leader, creating the clean industries, businesses and jobs of the future. And proud to be here fighting for the interests of our Pacific family,” he said.
Australia had pushed for a role at the climate summit, he said, “because we wanted to speak for the people of the world who need urgent action, including those from our Pacific family”.
Australia is the world’s second largest exporter of coal for burning in power stations and the largest exporter of coal for steelmaking. A fifth of the world’s exported LNG comes from Australia.
Albanese pointed to “significant successes” for the country on climate change, including doubling renewable energy generation in six years that accounted for half of the country’s electricity, and building one of the world’s biggest rooftop solar and battery markets.
Guterres and several countries are pushing for the talks to progress a proposal from last year’s Cop hosts, Brazil, for countries to develop detailed plans to move away from fossil fuels.
Guterres told the conference: “Leaders – and in particular those from developed countries – cannot keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5 degrees.”
He said to keep the globally-agreed goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C within reach, coal power had to fall by at least 75% by 2035.
Unabated coal power – that is, coal generated without safely capturing the carbon dioxide emissions – “must be all but phased out” by 2040, and oil and gas use cut by a third, he said.
“Every government must align its policies, investments and infrastructure plans accordingly. That starts with credible national roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels — protecting workers and communities.
“That means no new coal. No new oil and gas infrastructure that puts 1.5 degrees further out of reach.”

Qantas, Australia’s flag carrier, is gearing up to launch Project Sunrise in 2027, designed to take passengers from London to Sydney in just 22 hours. 

 
The route is expected to revolutionise long-haul travel, complete with game-changing features such as a ‘Wellbeing Zone’ and lighting scenes to reduce jet lag. 
However, as mere mortals, our bodies aren’t designed to spend such long periods of time in the air, 40,000 feet above sea level.  
So, to understand what actually happens to our bodies on a long-haul flight, Metro spoke with Dr Nikki Ramskill, private GP and founder of The Female Health Doctor.  
24-hour flight? Ready to complete it, mate. 
 
   
If you’ve ever travelled on a long-haul flight in economy, you’ll know it’s meant to test us (Picture: Shutterstock / Matej Kastelic) 
What happens to your body on a long-haul flight? 
According to Dr Ramskill, the body goes through different phases as the hours go on.  
During the first four, when you’re sitting for long periods (especially with your knees bent and very little movement), the calf muscles aren’t doing their job to help pump the blood back to the heart. 
‘This means blood can start to pool in the lower legs, which is why you may find your ankles and feet are quite swollen.’ 
Hours 4 to 8 
This is when the cabin environment starts taking its toll. 
‘Aircraft cabins are pressurised, but the pressure is still lower than we’re used to at sea level, which means there’s a slightly lower concentration of oxygen available to the body.’ But again, most healthy people cope with this. 
The air in the cabin is also very dry, which can leave passengers with dry eyes, nasal passages, skin and mouth. 
Elsewhere, ‘cabin pressure changes can cause the gas in the digestive tract to expand, leading to a feeling of bloating, discomfort or being rather gassy.’  

 
Dr Ramskill adds that sitting in one position can also lead to stiffness in the hips, lower back and neck. 

  
Hours 8 to 12 
Fatigue and sleep disruption become more noticeable here, as our natural body clocks start to clash with the environment we’re in. 
‘Our circadian rhythm dictates when we feel sleepy, alert and hungry,’ the GP states. But on an ultra-long-haul flight, you could be having a meal or trying to go to sleep at a time when your body would normally be doing something different.

This is Gill’s storyLocation: London, UKDisaster: UK heatwave, 2026Gill (not her real name), 43, is a teacher in London. In 2026, during the hottest summer on record, she suffered a seizure after experiencing heat exhaustion while teaching. The heatwave was made worse by the climate crisis. Continue reading...
articles.raw_meta: As a UK heatwave intensified in early summer this year, the health impacts began to worsen – This is Gill’s story
articles.jina_text:
Gill (not her real name), 43, is a teacher in London. In 2026, during the hottest summer on record, she suffered a seizure after experiencing heat exhaustion while teaching. The heatwave was made worse by the climate crisis.








 
  

The heat has always made me feel anxious and uncomfortable, but this year was different. The temperature was building up as the summer went on and as it was escalating it was becoming more and more frightening.
It was impossible to get any meaningful rest because I couldn’t fall asleep and when I did, I would wake up feeling suffocated because the air was so thick and dry and hot and there was nothing I could do to make myself feel better. Drinking water, using a fan, it didn’t help.
It got to the point where I would wake up feeling like I couldn’t breathe and with this rising sense of panic where I couldn’t really imagine how I was going to get through the day. I felt unsafe.
There was a lot of anxiety among my colleagues too. People were obviously very uncomfortable, they were worried about the kids, worried about themselves.
One day in late June I woke up and I was exhausted and was lacking the motivation that I normally have for work.


View image in fullscreen
Summer weather in Brockwell Park, south London, in August. Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PA
I got to work and my classroom was 30C. It used to be the photocopier room but because of demand for space they took the photocopier out. It’s a very small room with no windows. It was never designed to be a classroom, it’s got no ventilation.
No one was really learning and I was dealing with challenging behaviour and as the day went on I started to feel increasingly unwell to the point where I was dizzy and feverish and I had a really bad headache. I felt like I couldn’t concentrate on anything.
I was diagnosed with epilepsy about 20 years ago. It took about a year to get on top of it, but since then it’s not something that affects my life in any way, it’s extremely well controlled. But on this day, I had my first absent seizure since the diagnosis.
The best way to describe it is like pressing pause on the TV remote. I was on my lunch break and there was a pause and then it was like I restarted again a few seconds later.
I went to meet my colleague in reception, and she told me I had a lot of symptoms of heat exhaustion. I was feverish, I felt cold but my skin was really hot to touch, I was unable to regulate my body temperature and was fluctuating between being really hot and really cold.

AI datacentres plan on-site power stations on huge scale despite climate risks, research reveals


181GW of gas-fired capacity proposed for sites in US and Europe because of delays in connecting to national grids, says report




Developers of AI datacentres plan to build on-site climate-destroying gas power stations on a huge scale to meet their energy demands, research reveals.
Datacentres planned across the US, the UK and mainland Europe have proposals to build fossil fuel plants on-site to create 181GW of gas-fired capacity because of delays to connect to national grids, according to the findings. This is almost four times the total peak electricity demand of Great Britain.

The research by BloombergNEF says this “speed to power” will – if the planned rollout happens – emit about 345m metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent a year in the US, where 90% of on-site gas-fired power stations are planned. This is equivalent to annual greenhouse gas emissions from about 72.8m fossil fuel cars.


The report was published on Wednesday as global leaders gathered in Turkey for the 31st UN climate summit, where increasing electrification – ideally from clean sources – is a central part of discussions. However, a number of key European leaders, including from France and Germany, will not be at Cop31, instead heading to Dublin where EU leaders will hold their first dedicated AI summit on Friday.
Mark Daly, the head of datacentres and emerging tech at BloombergNEF, said: “The extraordinary economics around AI are making speed to power one of the most important priorities for defining constraints on datacentre developers.
“The climate outcome will depend not only on how much electricity these facilities use, but on how quickly grids can connect them and whether power systems add cleaner generation alongside that demand.”







Activists break into building site of Microsoft datacentre in Amsterdam

Read more
By 2035, the electricity demand of AI datacentres was predicted to almost quadruple to 2,354 terawatt-hours – equivalent to 7% of global electricity demand – the report said.
AI datacentres use a massive amount of electricity to power servers and cool equipment, and to run facility systems.


Daly said while the developers of the future datacentres claimed their gas-fired power supplies would be temporary while they waited for grid connections, once they were online, the economics could encourage them to continue generating energy, creating a longer-term fossil-fuel lock-in risk.
The report said ensuring new datacentres were connected to the grid was the more sustainable option. Fas

Motorists thinking of buying an electric car risk losing hefty discounts unless they act sooner rather than later.



The cost of an electric vehicle (EV) – including second hand cars and hybrids – is set to rise significantly as it is likely that mandated sales targets for manufacturers will be watered down.



EV makers currently offer discounts of several thousand pounds on cars and SUVs – the average discount last year was £2,800 – in order to meet the targets.



These discounts could take a significant cut if manufacturers are not under so much pressure to sell their stock, experts say. 



And, separately, if the Government decides to align with EU tariffs on Chinese EVs as part of efforts to get closer to Europe, it could add £12,600 to the cost of a Chinese model priced at £30,000. EVs produced in China are typically among some of the cheapest on the market.



Experts says the lowest price for electric cars is likely to be “right at this moment” and that they expect them to increase from 2027 and beyond.

The cost of an electric vehicle (EV) – including second hand cars and hybrids – is set to rise significantly as it is likely that mandated sales targets for manufacturers will be watered down. 
EV makers currently offer discounts of several thousand pounds on cars and SUVs – the average discount last year was £2,800 – in order to meet the targets.



 
These discounts could take a significant cut if manufacturers are not under so much pressure to sell their stock, experts say.  
And, separately, if the Government decides to align with EU tariffs on Chinese EVs as part of efforts to get closer to Europe, it could add £12,600 to the cost of a Chinese model priced at £30,000. EVs produced in China are typically among some of the cheapest on the market. 
Experts says the lowest price for electric cars is likely to be “right at this moment” and that they expect them to increase from 2027 and beyond.  
Higher prices may lead to fewer sales of new cars which would also feed through into the second-hand market, reducing the supply of vehicles on sale and checking the reduction in prices in this market.



 
The Government’s Zero Emissions Vehicle (ZEV) mandate requires car makers to ensure that 33 per cent of the new cars they sell in 2026 are electric, with the target rising each year to 80 per cent by 2030. Manufacturers that fall short face a £12,000 fine for every vehicle they miss the target by, although there are ways to avoid penalties, such as buying credits from rivals that exceed their targets or offsetting emissions elsewhere in their vehicle fleets. 
Companies that sell more EVs than required can earn extra income by selling these credits to manufacturers struggling to meet the targets. If the Government lowers the EV sales targets as expected, demand for the credits would fall, pushing down their value. That would hit firms such as Tesla and some Chinese brands, which rely heavily on EV sales and credit revenues, potentially leaving them with less scope to cut prices for consumers. 
Ben Westerman, director of policy and advocacy at Electrify Britain – a body which campaigns for electrification – told The i Paper: “Lowering targets will almost certainly contribute to raised electric car prices. Strong targets encourage carmakers to offer discounts on new models. As most people buy second-hand, fewer electric cars now will mean fewer affordable ones in the future.” 
What the discounts look like 
Car firms have been heavily discounting electric vehicles in order to hit the sales targets. For example, the all electric Volvo EX40 – a luxury SUV – is advertised with a £4,250 discount – meaning the £48,860 vehicle is on the road for £44,610. 
For cars priced under £37,000, the government is paying for an EV discount on new all electric cars of £3,750. This can also be combined with a manufacturer’s discount. An MG4 EV is available for £28,995, with a manufacturer’s discount of £1,500.

Full SummaryTurkey's hosting of the Cop31 summit in Antalya faces criticism due to the nation's continued investment in coal and fossil fuels despite its climate pledges. While the government promotes electrification and green industry, the expansion of major coal plants like Afşin-Elbistan has raised significant public health and environmental concerns among local residents.
On the veranda of a small house, Omer coughs as his wife serves up sweet tea and biscuits. The golden glow of late-afternoon sun peaks through nearby foliage and scatters across the floor – an idyllic scene, perhaps, but for a swell of black smoke pooling in the sky over us.
All day – and some say at night, too – emissions chug out in huge columns from alternating chimneys at the nearby Afşin-Elbistan coal plant. It leaves the air all around the surrounding plateau, in Turkey’s southern Kahramanmaraş region, feeling dry and heavy in the mouth and lungs. 
Now in his late fifties, Omer has worked at the vast plant for years, as well as living a stone's throw from it. His brothers also worked there, but in recent years, three have died – two from lung cancer and one of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a progressive lung condition that can be caused or worsened by long-term exposure to coal fumes. 





“I believe working at this plant killed them,” says Omer, pointing his finger towards it in indignation. “And I’m not going to see 65, I know that.”
Another brother is also living with COPD and asthma. According to Omer, his late brothers were between 55 and 61 when they died, and there was no previous history of these illnesses in his family. His father – who was also born in the village – lived to 97.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has welcomed a £12 billion investment in wind farms as he prepares to head to the Cop31 climate summit.




Energy company RWE and investment firm KKR have announced the funding which will deliver the Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore wind farms off the Norfolk coast.








The financing includes £1 billion from the state-owned National Wealth Fund.




Prime Minister Andy Burnham has welcomed a £12 billion investment in wind farms as he prepares to head to the Cop31 climate summit.




The wind farms are set to be delivering power by 2030, with construction set to begin early next year.




Mr Burnham said: “This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain.




“It is great news for billpayers because every turbine we put up is power under British control, not at the mercy of events on the other side of the world.




“With coastal communities from Scotland to East Anglia powering Britain’s future, the places that host this energy benefit from the jobs and opportunities that it brings.













“Our National Wealth Fund means that public investment is working alongside private capital to build homegrown energy and bring a return for the taxpayer. Because, for me, a clean energy future is one that brings down bills.”




Mr Burnham will join other world leaders at the United Nations’ Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, where he will deliver a speech on Thursday.

Andy Burnham has hailed a record investment in offshore wind, as the government tries to repair its green credentials after approving the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea.

Ed Miliband will tell the Cop31 UN climate summit on Wednesday that security and defence objectives are the new “frontier” of climate action, because the rapid heating of the planet will lead to food shortages, widespread economic disruption, migration and conflict.

Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow?


As the IUCN global conservation body prepares to update its red list of endangered species, scientists explain why calculating the true toll of a pandemic is so hard




It began with the brown skuas. The migratory seabirds had arrived on the sub-Antarctic island of South Georgia in 2023, harbouring a deadly passenger. Within months, the southern elephant seals that had come ashore to breed became sick. Mothers and newborn pups were weak and trembling, with many struggling to breathe. What followed was a horrific mass casualty event, caused by the highly infectious avian influenza (H5N1).
By 2025, more than 53,000 female elephant seals had died on South Georgia. That is especially alarming, scientists say, because the island is home to more than half of the global breeding population.

A highly potent strain of the bird flu virus, which first began circulating in the northern hemisphere in 2021, has now spread to four of the five main southern elephant seal populations. In some South Atlantic colonies, more than 90% of newborn pups have died, alongside about half of all adult females.


View image in fullscreen
A southern elephant seal with a pup at Gold harbour, South Georgia. By 2025, more than 53,000 female elephant seals had died on the island. Photograph: Ashley Cooper/Alamy
“This is a horror show for wildlife,” says Ruth Cromie, coordinator of a UN taskforce on avian influenza and wildlife. “The scale of mortality is absolutely unprecedented.”
In April, the mass deaths prompted the IUCN red list, the global authority responsible for assessing the extinction risks of wildlife, to downgrade the southern elephant seal’s conservation status by two categories, from “least concern” to “vulnerable”.
It was the first time a species has had its extinction risk raised explicitly because of H5N1.


View image in fullscreen
Dead elephant seals on South Georgia in January 2026. Photograph: Jane Younger
The IUCN listing notes that scientists suspect the global southern elephant seal population has declined by nearly a third, and models suggest many populations will take decades to recover. So far, scientists have found few antibodies to the disease among surviving animals.
The southern elephant seal is just one species that has suffered catastrophic die-offs since H5N1 began burning its way through the world’s wildlife, killing hundreds of thousands of animals, if not millions. Avian influenz

View image in fullscreen
Attendees pass a display highlighting the 1.5°C global warming threshold at the Cop31 conference in Turkey. Photograph: Bianca Otero/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock


Developing countries in limbo as rich nations delay new climate finance plans


Many governments are yet to set targets, leaving recipient countries struggling to plan and attract private investment




Developing countries have been left in limbo by the failure of some of the world’s biggest economies to flesh out their plans for new climate finance.
Poor countries are supposed to receive $300bn a year from the governments of industrialised nations by 2035, along with about $1tn from other sources, to help them cope with the effects of extreme weather and shift to a low-carbon future.

But many rich governments have not yet set out their targets and plans for providing climate finance beyond the end of this year or next. This gap is damaging because it means recipient countries cannot plan and makes it harder for them to attract private sector investment to supplement the public sector money.







UN chief urges Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia to turn fossil fuel promises into action

Read more
Analysis by the NRDC and E3G thinktanks seen by the Guardian shows that the developed world is broadly on track to meet the $300bn a year goal – known as the NCQG, or national collective quantitative goal – set at the Cop29 conference two years ago. By 2030 they should be providing about $229bn a year. The multilateral development banks should provide about $185bn of that.
Joe Thwaites, international climate finance director at the National Resources Defence Council, co-wrote the original analysis along with the E3G thinktank and told the Guardian that unless development banks and national governments made sharp cuts in the next round of financing, which is unlikely, then the level of finance needed by 2030 would be almost met.
“Most countries look in quite good shape on climate finance,” he said. “The problem is that they’re not being very public about it.”


If the EU continues its current provision of about $36bn a year (which is likely) then – taking into account the pledges already made by the UK, Canada and some other smaller countries – there would remain a gap of about $7bn to fill.
If a different president is in the White House, the US could make up some of the shortfall, along with Japan and Australia, which have yet to set out climate finance goals, according to Thwaites.
Further analysis by Carbon Brief suggested that if countries failed to implement any new climate finance after their current targets expire, the developing world would face cuts of 70% in bilateral finance (which excludes the development banks) from the rich world. But Thwaites said this was highly unlikely.

articles.jina_text:
Why are Britain’s streets still so polluted? Because the car industry dinosaurs do what they like, and politicians let them

George Monbiot



The transition to electric vehicles should be moving apace, but it is not. And why? Incompetence, expedience and cowardice




This is how it works. An industry puts tremendous effort into resisting change: lobbying governments, mobilising the media, pouring money into junktanks. It argues that a transition would threaten jobs, or damage the national interest, or harm poor people, while what it really fears is the cost of retooling its plants or developing new protocols. Then, when the inevitable cliff edge approaches, it whines that change is coming too soon. For reasons beyond its control, it isn’t ready, so the government must delay its plans.
This is what triggered the Dutch nitrate crisis, and the UK’s repeated “emergency” exemptions from the ban on a devastating class of pesticides. Now the same dynamic is driving the UK’s crisis over the transition to electric vehicles (EVs). The result is that, as the global climate summit, Cop31, begins, it looks as if our gift to the world will be a major, predictable and entirely avoidable increase in the UK’s greenhouse gas emissions.



Car manufacturers could have seen this coming more than 130 years ago, when the first electric automobiles were sold. For at least the past 30 years, as new electromotive technologies have progressed at speed, they plainly represented the future, and internal combustion engines, with their hard efficiency limits and vast impacts on human and planetary life, the past. Since 2010, it’s been obvious that China, which has not only seen the future but seeks to own it, would flatten our manufacturers like hedgehogs if they didn’t speed up. In 2023, the Conservative government gave automakers seven years to get their act together. And now they wring their hands and claim to be unprepared. To which the only reasonable answer is: tough.
But, unfortunately, this doesn’t seem to be the answer the government is giving. Instead, on Wednesday it’s expected to cut the target for zero-emission cars from 80% of new car sales by 2030 to approximately 60%. If so, this will be the latest in a series of concessions that governments have agreed since the Conservatives announced the deadline.
Both Conservative and Labour governments have permitted a series of “flexibilities” (otherwise known as loopholes). These allow companies to sell hybrid petrol-electric cars instead of purely EVs. They can also sell a lower proportion of EVs by 2030 on the promise that they’ll accelerate sales after that date. Now the government is also expected to extend the “flexibilities” to 2034, making a mockery of the promise to accelerate after 2030. One retreat after another.

articles.title: 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted
articles.raw_rss: Forecasters warn that this year's El Niño could be one of the strongest on record, with heavy rain and flooding in Kenya.
articles.raw_meta: Forecasters warn that this year's El Niño could be one of the strongest on record, with heavy rain and flooding in Kenya.
articles.jina_text:
"It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the 6ft [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya.
Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi.
The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water.
Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives.
"Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls. "When I see a picture of her, I feel uneasy, that's why I keep it far from me, so I don't see it."
With Kenya's short rainy season now starting, Shikoli tells the BBC she is afraid - especially following warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a new round of flooding.
"I feel like it can kill us. These houses aren't made of stone," says the 62-year-old. "They can fall on us, or the water can drown us."
Kibera - and Kenya more widely - are on the front line of preparations for the potential impact of El Niño.














Forecasters have warned that this year could see one of the strongest on record, bringing extreme weather to many parts of the world.
In southern Kenya, that means the threat of rains even more intense than usual.
Outside Shikoli's house, groups of men and women wearing high-visibility vests are shovelling and raking garbage out of the riverbed and disposing it far from the water.
This programme called Climate Worx, under the office of President William Ruto, is meant to rehabilitate Nairobi's rivers. Such exercises have intensified since August when warnings increased about the possible scale of this year's El Niño.


Rubbish clogging Nairobi's drains and sewers was seen as a major factor in the deadly floods earlier this year
Similar work to unclog drainage systems is ongoing across Nairobi, a sprawling city built on hilly ground crossed by three major rivers.
But the workers have a huge task on their hands.
Blocked drains and inadequate sewage systems were widely blamed for the high number of deaths after the floods earlier in the year, as the excess rainfall had nowhere to escape.










The Nairobi County disaster management chief, Bramwell Simiyu tells the BBC that drainage systems have been "untouched for many years" and that removing the rubbish from them will save lives.
Floods disproportionately affect informal settlements in Nairobi, especially those near rivers, like Kibera and Mathare.

articles.jina_text:
Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate activist who inspired global climate protests several years ago, said climate change is “threatening everything” and that “everything and everyone we love is at stake.”
In comments reported by AP, she told reporters in Antalya: “We should act to protect and benefit people rather than constantly sacrificing the global majority, and the very planet we are all living on, for a fortunate few to keep making unimaginable profits and maintaining geopolitical power,” she told reporters.
Cop31 is the first UN climate summit Thunberg has attended since the Cop26 conference in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2021, where she dismissed promises made by global leaders as “blah, blah, blah.”
Since then, fossil fuel emissions have continued to rise – though they flatlined this year – adding even more planet-heating gas to a beleaguered atmosphere. While many big polluters have taken steps to clean up their economies, none are doing so fast enough to keep global heating to the 1.5C Paris climate target.

Greenpeace has unveiled a giant limestone boulder carved into the likeness of Sir David Attenborough, which it plans to throw into the North Sea to deter bottom trawling.
Dubbed the “Attenboulder”, the sculpture was revealed aboard the campaign group’s ship Arctic Sunrise on the River Thames on Tuesday.


View image in fullscreen
The “Attenboulder” on the MY Arctic Sunrise. Photograph: Andrew McConnell/Greenpeace
It will join the boulders Greenpeace placed in the Southern North Sea marine protected area earlier this month, in protest at the lack of restrictions on fishing in most of it. The Marine Management Organisation has threatened legal action unless Greenpeace stops placing boulders.
The unveiling comes as Blue Planet III renews attention on ocean protection.
Will McCallum, Greenpeace UK’s co-executive director, said: “Right off our coasts the government still allows industrial fishing vessels to bulldoze the seabed and all of the incredible marine life it holds.
“These are supposed to be safe havens for wildlife – not killing grounds. The government’s inaction makes a mockery of the term ‘marine protected area’ and is an insult to Attenborough’s urgent work over many years.”

More than 700 groups ranging from trade unions to disability advocates have urged diplomats to prioritise a “just transition” for the people who will be hit hardest by a shift to a clean economy.

Solar panels can reduce your electricity bills for decades, but installing them typically costs several thousand pounds. The good news is that solar panel grants and other government-backed funding schemes could help cover some or all of the upfront cost, depending on your circumstances.
In 2026, eligible households can access free solar panels through schemes such as ECO4 and the Warm Homes: Local Grant. However, funding is generally targeted at lower-income households or properties with poor energy efficiency, and qualifying doesn't automatically mean you'll receive solar panels.
For homeowners who don't qualify for a grant, other financial support is available to reduce or spread the cost of solar panels, including the government's new Warm Homes Loan Scheme, zero per cent VAT on qualifying installations and payments for surplus electricity exported to the grid.

The Labour-led London authority is behind on its target to replace inefficient gas boilers with heat pumps in council-owned properties
Alamy/PA

Patrick Daly|Philip James Lynch, LDRS Reporter
2 hours ago

Hounslow Council is behind on 80 per cent of the measures needed to meet its ambitious 2030 net zero target, raising fresh doubts over whether the west London borough can become carbon neutral within four years.






Council documents show a series of flagship climate projects have stalled or fallen behind schedule, despite the authority declaring a climate emergency seven years ago.




The council, currently led by a minority Labour administration, declared a climate emergency in 2019 and adopted a climate action emergency plan five years later.





But one year on from its “refreshed” action plan, 80% of its policies are off track.




Its ambitious net zero target is 20 years ahead of the UK Government, which is aiming for the country to effectively be carbon neutral by 2050. 




There is a right-wing movement attempting to push back against net zero policies, which critics claim could stunt economic growth and lead to higher bills.








That is despite the UN warning recently, ahead of the major global Cop31 environmental conference taking place in Turkey this week, that the world will overshoot the key climate threshold of 1.5C warming above pre-industrial levels, beyond which extreme weather events is likely to become more intense and frequent.




In west London, the net zero pledge at highest risk of not being delivered is Hounslow Council’s aim to decarbonise the council’s entire operational estate. 


Hounslow House 
LDRS / Google Maps




The authority’s target includes replacing inefficient gas boilers with heat pumps, installing solar panels and installing energy efficacy measures.




However, only one of the council’s 37 buildings has been decarbonised, with this section of the project rated “high risk” because “the funding required to deliver decarbonisation of council operations to achieve net zero by 2030 is significant, and not currently identified or available”.




A further 29 assets have been partially decarbonised, and seven have not been decarbonised at all.




Hounslow has also committed to decarbonising 16,000 council-managed social homes by 2030. 




Progress on the move stalled this year, with only 150 homes fully decarbonised, and no further homes decarbonised in 2026.
